McCormack also praised the man who has been behind the organization of Peabody Golf Day.
"Over the past nine years, Joe O'Boyle has gotten the whip out and he's asked these volunteers to help out to make this day a success," McCormack said. "The commitment will always be there for the Salem Country Club to do our part to be part of the community of the city of Peabody."
Commitment to the community is the driving force behind the fundraiser.
"Back in 1995, we were celebrating our centennial just as the city was celebrating their bicentennial," explained the 83-year-old O'Boyle, a Salem CC member since 1967. While on the subject of inspiration, the fact that the creative writing
professor called me a born writer has further cemented my belief that I can make
it in such a competitive field. A writer's goal is positive feedback from the reader.
My teacher's comments, my grandmother crying upon reading a sad poem of
mine, and what I feel in my heart about my talent continually motivate me every
morning as I awake to be the best. Well, second to Dylan isn't all that bad, is it?
If I was a religious man I'd pray for the day when I can wake up in the
morning and be a writer - first and foremost, rather than a painter or landscaper.
To be able to push a pencil rather than a paintbrush. I often wonder what
wonderful compositions have been lost due to the fact that I have to work a job
with my hands rather than my brains. I have not found a job doing what I love yet
but at least I know that I'll know it when I see it. Until I catch my break all I can
do is dream towards the day when writing is my job rather than just my favorite
hobby. But that day will come because echoing in my ear is the word “Yeah!”

I am the ballplayer Shoeless Joe Jackson. I got my nickname back in 1908 when I was playing in Greenville, North Carolina. I was breaking in new spikes and I got blisters on my feet something awful. I asked the coach to sit out but we were shorthanded and he needed me to play. I played in socks and ended up hitting a triple when someone out in the stands yelled, “Shoeless, you son of a gun!” I guess the name stuck. During my stay in the Majors from ’08 to ’20 I had a lifetime average of .356 and we won the Series in ’17. The series of ’19, however, was much more complicated than the one we were in a couple of years before. Before the ’19 series I was known as “Shoeless” and people said that my corner of the outfield was “Where triples go to die.” A year later I was banned from baseball and when my name was spoken of people usually said “Say it ain’t so, Joe.”

The year of the ’19 Series, us Sox were the best team in the American League. We finished first and I ended up batting .351. During that season though, we were a divided team. There was a lot of hostility between Eddie Collins’ group of guys and Chick Gandil’s. Collins and his bunch thought that they were high class citizens and educated and stuff. They made around 15 thousand dollars a season. Us guys who weren’t as educated only made around 6 thousand. We were always getting low balled by the owner because we weren’t as educated as Collins and his buddies. That son of a bitch Cominsky

ARGUMENTATION: some basic terms and concepts
I. A proposition is a debatable claim; there are three basic types of propositions.
A. Proposition of fact is a debatable claim about the existence or occurrence of something.
Examples:
“Life forms exist on Mars.”
“John Doe is guilty of murder in the first degree.”
*Courtrooms debate propositions of fact.
B. Proposition of value is a debatable claim about the worth or value of a person, object, event, or idea.
Example:
“__________ is a great movie.”
C. Proposition of policy is a debatable claim about a proposal for civil change.
Examples:
“All Massachusetts State employees should take a 1% pay cut for this fiscal year.”
“An additional penny tax earmarked for education should be levied in Massachusetts.”
*Propositions of policy contain propositions of fact and value, because in order to decide what to do (policy), you must decide what the facts are (fact) and what they mean (value).

II. An issue is any potential point of conflict (or argument) specifically contained in a given proposition. These issues are phrased as questions. There are some standard or “stock” issues contained in all propositions.

A. Issues of definition are all conflicts or arguments that center around the meaning of the words or phrases in the proposition.
Example:
Proposition: “John Doe is guilty of murder in the first degree.”
Issues of definition: What is “murder in the first degree”?
a. What is sanity?
b. What is motive?
c. What is premeditation?

ANY GIVEN DAY

Another morning
As the sun comes up again
You drink a cup of coffee
Say hello to your friend

Take a peek at the paper
Any good news today?
Seems like nothing but trouble
So face down it will stay

Eight o'clock in the morning
As your cubicle cries out your name
You sit down in front of your computer
The monotony remains the same

Another sip of coffee
The stacks of papers stay in your drawer
So many places you'd rather be
Find yourself asking what and who are you doing this for?

Ten years of marriage to your work
Yet how could this be so engraved into your life?
Dropped off the kids at school
A kiss goodbye to your loving wife

You really need a vacation
Tried to get the week off but you couldn't go
The boss promised you next week
You should have pushed stronger but how could you expect to know

Yet you're still sitting here
Up on the sixty sixth floor
You could have been ascending on a plane
Maybe heading off towards Europe to go explore

Gazing out your window
You see that the New York skyline's so pretty
And your office is such a bore
Suddenly you see a sight among sights
Never seen a plane flying so low before

This day was coming

WORDS:
YouTube - Broadcast Yourself.
    
    hi tom...need your help
    
    i'm gonna tell a little about myself
    and if you can create a poem of it
    i will try to turn it into a song
    
    i've just wrote my last will and testament and
    i want to express my love for my children
    I have two little boys jacob and luke aged 3 and 2
    and a baby daughter called ella, she will be aged 1 soon
    
    i'm 39 years old
    
    I also have a 19 year old daughter roxanne, from a previous relationship
    I have lost contact with her and would like her to know that
    i would have liked to have been around while she grew up and that
    i miss her very much-this subject really hurts me when i think
    about what a great relationship we could have had.
    
    i want to express the best time a father and daughter could have had
    if she hadn't have been unreachable all these years.
    
    ive had experiences such as being in the army and times i've had to think
    
    about what i wished would have happened-just before i put my life at risk
    
    i've had experiences that made me grow up fast
    
    my partner helen has been with me nearly ten years now-through thick
    and thin
    i love her so much but find it hard to tell her how much.
    an accident whilst driving at work in 2005 gave me slight brain damage-i
    lost my personality and identity and became withdrawn
    i've lost my job in the civil service because i cannot work anymore-and i
    don't take my young children out to parks and things like that
    because my brain keeps ticking on never ending signals-it takes me a
    long time to do anything from beginning to end-so i put things off. i'm
    always in a state of confusion.
    
    i have something wrong goin on inside my body aswell and am too afraid
    
    to go doctors-so just incase anything happens to me
    i would like all these important people to know how much i love them
    from deep
    within my heart
    
    sorry to burden you with this request tom, but you write so well
    i thought you might like the challenge and i'm just lookin for the best
    writer to
    write words to say that i care about them all-so that i can put a really
    good
    song together with your help.
    
    i don't normally speak this frankly to anyone-it seems easier that you
    don't
    know me-and if i don't act now-i may never get it done.
    
    i dont mind if a poem is just 4 lines long or 4 pages
    i'll make sure your name is on as the writer-i'll just add chords and sing it
    
    if you can't do it thats fine and if you try but can't do it thats fine. i feel
    kind of selfish asking you this and am on the brink of deleting the
    message-thats how low i feel.
    
    i appreciate you reading this
    and keep sending the stuff you send-i like jd and i really enjoy reading
    and listening to the songs people compose from your words
    
    goodnight tom

There is a big difference between a group and a team. A group is a cluster of people whereas a team is a group that has been organized to get a job done. For a group to become a team, the members must have a high degree of trust, mutual respect for ideas, open communication, equal participation, and constructive confrontational skills. As you might imagine, a team does not automatically form from a group - it takes a lot of hard work on the part of the group members and they have to WANT to succeed as a team.

This process is not easy. The dynamics of a group becoming a team include four phases:
1. Forming - awareness and acceptance of others
2. Storming - conflict concerning leadership and style of decision making
3. Norming - cooperation results from involvement and support
4. Performing - achievement of the desired productivity

ODE TO JASON
(A FALLEN HERO)
This is a story about a boy whose dog ran away
Who, during a snowstorm, went out to play
Jason set out to find a loved one - no matter what the cost
But as the dog came home the little boy became lost
When you're a fourth grader finding a dog is no easy task
Should you risk your life for a pet? It depends on whom you ask
The fact that Jason said yes should come as no surprise
He loved that dog to pieces you could see it in his eyes
Little Jason was a hero so he set out through the snow
So it saddens my heart deeply to tell his tale of woe
What a brave little soul, right up until the end
What a brave little soul to go search for his friend
A little bit of inspiration is what he left behind
He listened to his heart, paid no attention to his mind
And right before he left our world with the situation oh so grim
The last thought that filled his head - his dog would do the same for him
The saddest of it all and the reason why we cried
If not for the heart of an angel he never would have died
When you think of him in memory try to wipe away your tears
And remember him for what he was which is wise beyond his years

FOLLOWING THE BLIND
Such a waste of time...
Following the blind
Open up your eyes
Haven't you realized?

'Tis better to lead them...
And still be breathing
Than it is to follow
And be the one left bleeding

Never wading in the springs of freedom...
And not understanding these things I speak of
Contemplating something hollow and misleading

And it brings many things...
Such as a false disguise by a gypsy king
In his lies we discover many truths...
Through his eyes we uncover his abuse
And his song of sorrow so many sing

For only a fool would break the sole rule...
Of the creator of thought
The earth shaker
The maker of everything
And all that there is to believe in or be bought
Is there really a tomorrow?

- If there is someone who has fallen in love with you (like me) then there are some things that you should avoid saying and/or doing around that person (like me). A lot of this involves some common sense that someone with blonde hair may or may not possess. For instance, if some one (like me) writes you a poem about their undying love for you and in that poem you are referred to as an angelic figure then there are roughly two responses that would be typical:

Response one - This response would be a friendly thankyou in which the subject of adoration (you) politely accepts the gift of words and meanings but makes it clearly known that there in no interest in persuading the desired aim (love) that the poet (me) expresses for his subject of adoration (you). If a blue mountain card is used then graphics should be plain and friendly and attempt to use images which contain very little imagery and symbolism that a gifted poet could easily pick up on.

Response two - This response would be one of gratitude, but more importantly, reciprication. This response would indicate a mutual feeling of love and some level of adoration. A response of this nature would evoke more poetry of the same nature and even stronger feelings by the poet (me) for the subject of adoration (you). If a blue mountain card was sent then the graphics would contain colorful and vivid images. In a response of this type then the images presented would be of a symbolic nature in which objects or images might include hearts, angels, or ROSES.

Your response - From the eyes of a poet, your response is looked at as a mixed signal. The words are perfectly in tune with response one where as the word "love" is not mentioned and there is no expression of mutual endearment on the basis of romance. However, when imagery is taken into consideration, the feelings of response one are questioned. A symbol of a rose goes hand in hand with love and romance. Therefore when a poet (me) receives a blue mountain card with one image from response two and a messege from response One then his mind twists and bends and his perplexion drips out of his brain through ear from his brain. When this happens then the poet's health becomes uncertain for this is a strange condition.

The poet believes that the blue mountain card comes only from the intentions that a response one would represents. But when a rose appears things get strange and wheels start spinning. Please refrain from blue mountain cards for awhile until you practice on some other people first. It may be a good idea to try something a little less demanding such as an email like this, for example. Typing is easy and if you're having some trouble with certain words than I suggest consulting a dictionary. Please take what I say as the truth and may it help you out in the future. Please respond via email or telephone or letter.

Thank You, Love Tom

Dear Rachel,
Here it is, no more beating around the bush. I Love you very, very much. But not as much as you love me. Who do I blame? Your mom, for conditioning you to go so much without love that once you find some of it you hold on to it for dear life, hoping that it will give to you what she never could. I almost felt like a "mother" to you, trying to always do the best and trying not to be selfish like her. I now realize that wasn't my place nor should have I tried to take it, but I felt someone had to. I blame Kristin for stealing my heart and creating a situation where the chips were stacked against you from day one, a situation in which you could never compete, even though if placed in a fair and square deal you would have rose miles ahead of the competition. I blame myself for putting you in the whole situation, even though that is the only thing I regret about our time together. But I now believe that this maybe for the best, after all. You deserve someone who will give you a fair deal from day one, a situation which I could not provide. I prevent you, whether you know it or not, from having a shot at true inner peace and happiness. For from now on you will always feel uneasy and unsure even if we were to try to give it another go. That is why I am now writing the final chapter in this Romantic Drama. Unfortunately happy endings only happen in the movies. I love you very much and would like no greater treasure in the world than to remain a part, as big a part as you'll let me, in your life. You are, without a doubt, my best friend. To lose you as a friend would hurt me as much as losing me as a boyfriend will hurt you (if not greater-for it is worse to lose a whole than a part). I am deeply saddened by this whole chain of events and would do anything not to hurt you. Because of this fact I am afraid to hurt you anymore than I already have. Please contact me by any means necessary, but please don't leave my life, for I will never give up trying to be your best friend again. I miss you and love you and have to do what's best for you even if it means hurting you now, I'm sorry.

Love,
Tom

The Quick Version:

I've been writing poems meant to be used as song lyrics ever since I was 17 years old and heard Bob Dylan's LIKE A ROLLING STONE on the radio in my father's minivan. Shortly after that I got drunk, blacked out and totaled the minivan when I hit a telephone pole at a rather high rate of speed. I crawled away and was largely unhurt but the engine was now riding shotgun. A foot to my left and I'd have been dead. If my friend came with me then today he would have no legs. That's when I became a public servant and dedicated my life to trying to making a difference in this world. I've been doing that for the last 18 years or so... on my own dime... full-time... all while hiding behind a computer screen... and now it's time to show you what I have got... no more hiding – I'm looking to take it LIVE to THE PEOPLE, THE MUSICIANS AND THE SINGERS THEMSELVES.

I put out a book of 130 poems (with commentary) inviting musicians from all over the world to turn my words into songs. That was in 2008. I didn't have any songs at this point. I put videos of my poems on YouTube and found artists (or artists found them) and...

Today I have had 130 songs made from my lyrics. That's about seven hours' worth of original music, right there. The enclosed CD has 22 of them – a nice assorted sampler. My website is filled with goodies...

My current book of poems waiting for music now has over 400 poems in it. At least 20 albums worth of songs are just waiting for musicians and singers. I want to start by creating or taking over a bar or venue and naming it SONGWRITERS' or joining a current establishment where I can use this place as a central location to create new songs by day (with audience participation and feedback, of course) in person and have musicians play the songs at night. There are a million possibilities and ways to go and potential offshoots of this idea but that's the main idea. It can start as tiny as a hole in the wall bar and restaurant idea or as big as a multimilion dollar investment opportunity... it can start with local musicians or big names in the industry...

Think of it like this – We all have our favorite filmmakers, right? But who has a favorite songwriter who acts as the voice behind the songs but NOT as the singer or musician themselves? In essence, I create a "song script" and then find the proper actors or actresses (in this case singers or musicians) to fill the part. That allows me, as a writer, to write without limits and if there is a story that needs to be heard then I can tell it and worry about whom re-tells it later... TOTAL FREEDOM.

This is just the very tip of the iceberg of ideas that I have but this one is the one that is easiest to start as I begin getting myself ready to sell the only thing that I have – and that's me! But luckily, that's a lot...

Enjoy and thank you for your time. My website is brianrainstorm.com

Tom
(415) 385 - 2774

P.S. The free book is one I just put out... I write, too. I will be in the SF area on October 1st for a few weeks and my name is Tom Jensen although I now write under the name of Brian Rainstorm.

Maids in the morning sweeping up broken glass
Long left dreams of a shattered past
Golden cup full of life spilled to the floor
A man who once had riches now lives poor
Some men live long and some die young
Some carry heavy burdens, some carry none
When you shadow box you sometimes bruise
When you fight yourself sometimes you lose
Walking down the spiral staircase that is mad my mind
Passing all the memories that I've left behind
If you see the same things enough it can make you blind
Be careful of what doors you open and what you'll find
Some patterns are so hard to break that they end up breaking you
Anyone who's ever worn those shoes knows that this is true
All by myself is where I found myself
I looked around and saw no one else
Pleasure that was promised evolved into pain
The sun changed to clouds then turned to rain
It was as if my clock had stopped and every day remained the same
As if all the roosters died and the man in the moon he never came
A man in the cemetery digging his own grave
A man thrown overboard with no chance of being saved
Just like a speeding train with no track ahead
Playing Russian roulette with the chamber full of lead
Going down a one way street the wrong way
No planning for a future, living day to day
I was trapped in quicksand and started sinking
My life stood on the brink and I started thinking
I must be going crazy I must be living my mind
I better get it together or I'll die before my time
So much I have yet so much I've thrown away
I can't wait tomorrow as everything begins today

The road leads uphill but I know I will sustain

**[Top Center/Right - Poem 3]**
WILTED ROSE
UNTITLED
On the table - a twelve inch blade
As night creeps in as black as blades
Would it really matter, one slip of the knife?
Would anyone notice, a worthless life?
Her inner voice has let her down
Left alone with no one around
With all the pain built up inside
Now discovered with nowhere to hide
From some pains you can never run away
Though sometimes forgotten, the scars will always stay
For sometimes there's no escape
And all it takes is a simple mistake
To burn down the mansion you built
And to knock the clown off his stilts
She lies on the floor - last thoughts so quilted
Clutching a rose now fallen wilted

UNTITLED
On the table - a twelve inch blade
As night creeps in as black as spades
Would it really matter, one slip of the knife?
Would anyone notice, a worthless life?
Her inner voice has let her down
Left alone with no one around
With all the pain built up inside
Now discovered with nowhere to hide

From some pains you can never run away
Though sometimes forgotten, the scars will always stay

And all it takes is a simple mistake
To burn down the mansion you built
And to knock the clown off his stilts
She lies on the floor, last thoughts so guilted
Clutching a rose now fallen wilted

Common Ground

---

LYNNFIELD — Discipline, dedication and self-motivation are usually the words associated with competitive running. Teamwork, however, is a major role that did play a rarity, although it did play a role during last Friday's 36th annual Social Club Scholarship Road Race in Lynnfield.
Peter Mallett, a 20-year-old junior at the University of New Hampshire, recorded the fastest time at 15:41 while his fellow UNH training partner, Steve Meinelt, finished just a second behind at 15:42 in the 3.1-mile race. Mallett willingly acknowledged the part that Meinelt, also 20, played in the race.
"He gave me the win. His job was just to go out there and pull me," said Mallett, a Manchester, N.H. native whose aunt lives in Lynnfield. "He's my training partner and he wanted to do better shape than I am right now."
Mallett and Meinelt are two of the anchors of the cross country team at UNH and generally run about 70 and 100 miles a week, respectively. Over the summer they try to run together twice a week. Meinelt's motivation for the race was not a selfish one.
"[I was running] strictly for my buddy," said Meinelt, who decided to run the route a second time after crossing the finish line. "I was helping him out. I told him before that I was going to do it twice. I'm thinking of doing a 10-miler so I wanted to go a little further. I figured I'll help him and then I'll just do it again."
Mallett was running the race for a third time.
"Last year I was dehydrated and went out the back door," he added. "This year I used it as a tune-up race."
Meinelt's selfless act personified a race in which the overall goal is to raise scholarship money for graduating seniors as much as lowering finishing times.
As for the women's winner, it was up to Amy Wallace to defend her family's name. With a winning time of 20:10, she did just that.
Shawn Wallace, Amy's younger brother, had won the men's division the last two years, but had to sit out this year's race with an injury. Originally from Wakefield, Wallace still had plenty of familiar faces surrounding her during the race, even though her brother was forced to watch from the crowd.
"I'm here cheering on these guys. They're my idols," Shawn said.
Amy's older brother, Bill Wallace, a science teacher at Lynnfield High School, ran the race while pushing his daughter in a stroller. Amy's mother, Judy, also competed this year and said, "I am very proud of her. I am proud of my son who ran with my granddaughter, too."

The Reeds' wrestling roots can be traced back to Vinny, a 1997 graduate and the first Reed to be inducted into the Wrestling Hall of Fame.

"My brother Vinny started wrestling," explains Sean Reed, the senior tri-captain who is 25-1 this year and 105-46 in his career, which places him 18 wins behind Lynnfield High School graduate Randy Greenstein, the school's all-time leader in career wins with 123. "And then Tony [a 1999 Lynnfield High School graduate who fell one win short of joining his brothers] kind of got into it and I went to their matches a lot. "I would have to say that Brendon was the best wrestler among all of the Reeds. Three times he's wrestled at states and three times he's placed...that's tough."

Kimball, a two-time state-place finisher who wrestled as both a 135 and 145-pounder, also comes from a wrestling family, first being exposed through his older brother Matt.

Kimball, a business administration major at Merrimack College, said "I think that when you put yourself around great people that only great things are going to happen. With Coach Stone, Coach Winslow and all of the other wrestlers there was a formula for success and it was fantastic. It just goes to show, I won just four matches as a freshman and as long as you keep putting in that work and keep showing up you are going to be successful. I almost quit as a freshman. I didn't understand the process of putting in the hard work and appreciating the time that it takes to improve. "To be in the Hall of Fame with guys like Chas, Sal and Brendon is just unbelievable," continued Kimball, who ranks ninth all-time in career wins with a record of 86-61, "I don't think it's too far of a reach for anybody because I was nothing when I started. As long as you show up, you're committed and you put in the effort then you're going to be successful."

The postponement of the ceremony also allowed Shepherd-Hill's wrestlers a chance to see the induction of Gesamondo, their assistant coach, who is seventh on the career wins list with a record of 95-41. Gesamondo, who presently plays baseball at Nichols College, illustrated his coach's point about the importance of good teammates.

"Luke Kimball not only was a great co-captain with me, but he's also one of my best friends. I think that he was half of my success, especially at states. I would have been knocked out in the second round. I had a tough match, but Luke gave me the good old 'get tough and if you lose I'm going to beat you up' so I had to get tough."

Ryan, a junior majoring in business at Suffolk University, explained that wrestling "gives you skills in so many different ways. You come and you're working out for yourself, you want to be the best you can be, but at the same time you're working out for your team. There are no excuses out there on the mat. If you lose then you're going to be your fault...nobody else's.

"I played football, where you have 11 other guys on the team," said Ryan, who was a state finalist at the 171-pound level as a senior and finished his career 73-40, which places him 11th all-time. "If you lose then there's a couple of other guys to point your finger at. Here, it's all you. You didn't work out in practice; you missed an opportunity, it shows you how to take responsibility!"

Hearing on retired teachers' health insurance proposal Monday night

by Robert Curtin

LYNNFIELD — The Board of Selectmen will take up the issue of whether to switch retired teachers' health insurance from the state Group Insurance Commission to the town plan on Monday, August 11.

The selectmen will meet at 7:30 p.m. at the Lynnfield High School media center.

The committee to proceed the meeting was proposed by selectman William Gustus at the July 23 meeting.

Gustus said that while the town and state plans differ in some respects, the town plan is generally equivalent to and in some respects better than that plan retired teachers now have. He urged retired teachers to review the plans to best suited their particular needs. That to end, Gustus mailed a detailed report on the provisions of the state and town plans to all retired teachers.

Chairman of the Board of Selectmen Robert Whalen said it is the board's intention to vote on the matter after the hearing but during the same meeting.

The hearing will also include a vote of the retired teachers present; although state law requires that vote, it is not binding of the Board of Selectmen.

To make the change from the state to the town system, the Board of Selectmen would have to rescind the 1972 acceptance of a local option of state law.

At the July meeting, Gustus selected that when the town moved in 1972 retired teachers were moved to the state system, insurance-wise. Since that time, the state has increased the cost of insurance to the town.

Recently, however, the state has increased deductibles and co-payments for insurance for retirees and increased the percentage retirees must pay for one type of plan. "Currently, teacher retirees pay more in copays and deductibles than town employees and retirees," said Gustus.

The recent changes by the state Group Insurance Commission, effective July 1, have retirees now paying 100 percent of the Medicare Part B premium, which is a portion of the state's managed care plan. Of the town's retired teachers, 71 are enrolled in this plan. As a result of the change, said Gustus, retirees on this plan went from paying 12.5 percent of the overall premium to 27 percent. Another change requires retirees to pay the entire difference in cost between generic drugs and brand-name drugs if their physician requires the brand name.

For years, retired teachers paid less for health insurance than did town employees and retirees. "That situation was reversed over the last few years," said Gustus.

The state, in sharing the cost, also cut the town's share of retiree health insurance costs and a higher rate.

Gustus said that both the state and the town plans offer Blue Cross/Blue Shield products, and while the benefit packages offered may differ in certain respects Gustus noted that the differences could make one plan preferable to another for individuals, based on their specific needs. But he said that on the whole, the town plans are equivalent to, and in some cases better than, the state plans. "In many cases, the town plan is superior," he said.

Teachers at the July meeting thanked the selectmen and Gustus for taking the time to share the details of the proposal, but were concerned that the board in the future would reduce the town's share of premiums in the future unilaterally.

Common Ground
---
LYNNFIELD — Discipline, dedication and self-motivation are usually the words associated with competitive running. Teamwork, however, is a major role that did play a rarity, although it did play a role during last Friday's 36th annual Social Club Scholarship Road Race in Lynnfield.
Peter Mallett, a 20-year-old junior at the University of New Hampshire, recorded the fastest time at 15:41 while his fellow UNH training partner, Steve Meinelt, finished just a second behind at 15:42 in the 3.1-mile race. Mallett willingly acknowledged the part that Meinelt, also 20, played in the race.
"He gave me the win. His job was just to go out there and pull me," said Mallett, a Manchester, N.H. native whose aunt lives in Lynnfield. "He's my training partner and he wanted to do better shape than I am right now."
Mallett and Meinelt are two of the anchors of the cross country team at UNH and generally run about 70 and 100 miles a week, respectively. Over the summer they try to run together twice a week. Meinelt's motivation for the race was not a selfish one.
"[I was running] strictly for my buddy," said Meinelt, who decided to run the route a second time after crossing the finish line. "I was helping him out. I told him before that I was going to do it twice. I'm thinking of doing a 10-miler so I wanted to go a little further. I figured I'll help him and then I'll just do it again."
Mallett was running the race for a third time.
"Last year I was dehydrated and went out the back door," he added. "This year I used it as a tune-up race."
Meinelt's selfless act personified a race in which the overall goal is to raise scholarship money for graduating seniors as much as lowering finishing times.
As for the women's winner, it was up to Amy Wallace to defend her family's name. With a winning time of 20:10, she did just that.
Shawn Wallace, Amy's younger brother, had won the men's division the last two years, but had to sit out this year's race with an injury. Originally from Wakefield, Wallace still had plenty of familiar faces surrounding her during the race, even though her brother was forced to watch from the crowd.
"I'm here cheering on these guys. They're my idols," Shawn said.
Amy's older brother, Bill Wallace, a science teacher at Lynnfield High School, ran the race while pushing his daughter in a stroller. Amy's mother, Judy, also competed this year and said, "I am very proud of her. I am proud of my son who ran with my granddaughter, too."

The Independence of John Brown
---
As the morning sun begins its rise overhead the sparrows sit atop
the old apple tree as they do every morning at about this time. The steady
chirping added to the whistling of the warm breeze are the only sounds that
can be heard this early in the morning. The busy sparrows can be seen
diving from their boughs toward the dying grass in their daily search of
worms. They pick about the parched earth for even the slightest morsel of
food and equally small insect. Food around these parts is hard to come by,
even the small amount it takes to feed such a bird as the sparrow. Once,
on this exact spot, stood a bird feeder and even a birdbath, both filled
almost daily. Though the feeder and bath are still there, they have become
broken and empty over time. The last time they were filled with food and
water was before the life of the present sparrows now residing on the limbs
on the old apple tree.
Not far from the apple tree is a small fenced in horse corral, though
indistinguishable now. The beams of wood that once surrounded the
perimeter have long fallen to the ground; the splits and cracks in the wood
along with gray discoloring reveal the wear and tear blended with the
beating of the hot sun. Once, the foundation stood strong and each beam
carefully fit interlocked with one another creating a strong and sturdy
stable. Sometime ago a beautiful Arabian, palomino horse could be seen
galloping around the field with the sun glistening across its golden body. At
---
sunset, the flaxen mane and tail of this magnificent animal stood so bright
that even if covered by the darkest shadow the color would resemble that
of the moon. Its coat was always clean and his mane and tail brilliantly
white and always combed. A full trough of clean water and a bucket of
oats always available. And as the stable became dilapidated and gradually
decayed over time, so did the life of this once spectacular animal. Its mane
and tail slowly darkened to a grim, dirty gray like that of the beams of his
own stable. The water trough and food bucket diminished from full to half
full, to bare. Once rippling muscles turned to skin and bones. A large
rectangular stone can be seen in the middle of the stable marking its final
resting-place, a foot away from where he fell.

The door to the cabin stands slightly ajar, the lower hinge of the
door hanging on by only a single nail. The weathered paint, seemingly
aged, is peeling off in every direction if not bare already. Broken and
shattered is every other pane of glass on all five windows located around
the doorway. The wind howls through the cracks of broken glass,
searching for the quickest escape from the confinements of the walls. The
steps leading up to the front door are contorted and the planks of wood
slightly bent. The rail on the left side is missing, the other so weak that a
strong breeze makes it sway to the same rhythm as the trees. This once
spectacular home belonged to John Brown.

I remember as a young boy I would frequently stop by these parts.
John would always have little tasks for me to do around his yard. Raking
---
leaves, chopping up firewood and I even helped him build his horse corral.
After my father died, when I was ten, I adopted John to be my father figure.
This was 10 years ago, and these 10 years were not kind to John Brown.
John was a man’s man; a carpenter, a mason, and like many men
from these parts, a farmer. There was nothing he couldn’t fix or grow. I
remember him telling me, “Little John, someday you’ll be big and strong
and you’re gonna become my partner. With my brains and your brawn we’ll
be rich.” After he said this I would stay awake in bed and wonder what that
would be like. Wondering whether we’d be master carpenters building a
new home for the governor or perhaps farmers growing our famous
popcorn. I even came up with a “corny” slogan: John and John’s famous
popcorn, “We ain’t stoppin’ until it’s poppin’.” I had a lot of free time on my
hands.
John was a family man. Every Sunday his wife, his three daughters,
two sons and himself would pick me up and we’d head down to the Second
Southern Baptist Church. We’d always sit in the third pew on the left. The
reverend would always smile at us when he came up to preach, as if to
say, “There’s John Brown, faithful John Brown, sure as the sun would rise,
he would be sitting in that very pew.” That’s the way he was, always early
and always faithful. If he said that he would meet you at 8:00, he’d be
there at 7:55 sharp.
Men like John Brown aren’t created out of thin air; there’s something
in the gene pool. Some type of knowledge, a sixth sense, passed down
---
from generations, father to son. I never met his father but John told me that they were both cut from the same cloth. Both were hardworking, independent, and the type to paint a masterpiece out of two colors. I swear he could build a palace out of junk just lying around his backyard. He once built a doghouse out of an old refrigerator and roof shingles. That dog would rather sleep in that damn refrigerator than a king-size bed. It’s as if the dog was proud that John made that house just for him. I can see why, I was proud just being with John. I could hear the gears turning in his head as he thought. Just standing a few feet away from him, I became smarter.

Unfortunately, this “I can do anything by myself” mentality lead John down a winding road. One summer’s night, I stopped by to see him and I noticed that a couple of shingles from his rooftop had blown off during the night’s strong wind. He asked me to help him fix them the next afternoon after school but I had to help my mother do chores. I told him I could help him the next day, a Saturday, and he said all right. But, being the strong, independent man that he was, he couldn’t wait. He decided to take on this venture by himself.

The roof had a steep slant to it and I remember that the next day was quite windy. No matter, John just went on with his work as he had hundreds of times before, being a carpenter and all. He was carrying up a heavy load of shingles and upon reaching the summit of the ladder, he lost his balance. Down came the shingles and down came John Brown. Roughly 30 feet he fell, landing with a thud and a snap. Later the doctors
---
told us that the snap was John's left leg and the thud his 12th Thoracic
Vertebrae severing his spinal chord at the point.
This man who had been, until now, so independent and free, was
suddenly thrust into his darkest nightmare. The broken leg was not the
problem, but the fracture of the smaller bone in his back was catastrophic.
The fracture, which severed his spinal cord, caused paralysis of John
Brown's body from the waist down. This man, my hero and father figure,
whom I'd earlier thought to be invincible, became powerless. Dependence
was not a word he knew the meaning of unless it pertained to someone
else. A man who always lit your cigarette and carried your groceries would
now need all those favors returned. How could he do that when the very
nature of his manhood prevented that from happening? He once told me
that he almost chopped off his pinky at work one day. He joked, "If I lost a
finger they might as well take my whole arm because I need that little finger
just as much." A carpenter without the use of his legs would be similar to a
singer with no voice; at least that's the way it seemed to John Brown.
The coming months were a nightmare. John first turned to booze to
cover his shattered dreams and declining passion for life. He bet that no
one expected any great things from a drunk and he felt in his present
condition to be worthless. Even though he would try to smile when his
children were near frowns always followed their departure. Since the
doctors told him his paralysis was permanent he began to lose hope. The
life he knew was gone and anything less deemed unacceptable.
---
The simplest tasks drove him half-crazy when he couldn't do them
with ease. When tying his shoes his children would have to help him. He
felt the cold irony about this for he was the one who taught his kids to tie
bows. Even though he was a brilliant man he felt as if he was reverting
back to childlike form because of his paralysis.
The drinking eased his mind somewhat yet when he realized he was
drinking more with each passing day he swore it off completely. He told his
wife "This isn't who I am. I'm not the town drunk sitting in his stool yelling at
the bartender to make him another drink. I'll die before that fate comes my
way." The doctor took notice to John's situation and kept a watchful eye on
him. The doctor knew him to be a good man and told John he needed to try
a craft or hobby to occupy his mind. His wife agreed with high optimism.
The decision was made for John to try his hand at designing houses. Even
though he couldn't lay foundations or put up shingles he became
guardingly excited at keeping his trade alive. He hoped that if he could feel
enough satisfaction through his work that he'd actually be happy to be
alive. He'd have the strength to get through another day.
Before the accident John had a good name in the community. Just
as he always lent his time and knowledge to anyone in need they were
more than happy to repay him. When news about John's new hobby
spread through the town he quickly became overwhelmed with offers.
Affluent members of the town finally decided it was time for an extra room
or new porch. Poorer members suddenly found the need for a shed or
---
even doghouses. The giving and caring nature of John's friends and
acquaintances uplifted his spirits and for the first time since his fall he felt
useful. He spent hours upon hours drawing up designs and converting feet
to centimeters and millimeters. The busyness of his day slowly dulled his
pain and he no longer felt like a helpless child needing help tying his
shoes. John was a man again.

The support from John's friends and acquaintances could only last
for so long. At about the same time John was really getting a knack for his
new line of work the phones stopped ringing. It seems that they all helped
him so much during the beginning of his injury that there were no projects
left for him to do. The people had given him all the work they could. The
demand in the town that was left for building was for actual laborers, not
creators. John again became unhappy, but being a smart man, he knew
this fountain of work would soon dry up. Only not this soon.

As jobs for John became few and far between the Brown family
decided a role reversal would be in order. John's wife had taken a job as a
secretary in a lawyer's office a couple miles down the road in neighboring
Shelbyville. She worked six days a week trying to support their family of
seven. After John accepted the fact that he was not the bread winner
things went surprisingly smooth. His children took up his idle time and even
though money was tight love and family time replaced it. This kept his mind

A Hard Rain's Gonna Fall
---
The smoke from a half lit cigarette waves aimlessly through the air. A light brown guitar sits in the corner awaiting the delicate touch of it's master. Three empty notebooks sit atop the table curiously wondering what will fill their blank pages. Will there be small sketches of beautiful young women or perhaps some silly verses about how everybody must get stoned? An old weathered, green chair, still feeling the pain of a dropped cigarette, reminisces about the time it's owner, the master, once sat for what seemed like an eternity trying to capture the soul of a man named Hollis Brown. An old, rusty razor lays, forgotten, in a corner clutching on to one last piece of cocaine. A broken guitar string sits beneath a pile of trash still humming the melody of what it prays comes true in "Forever Young", and in the state of mind that it will never be thrown away. 

A familiar face appears from behind a closed door. All of the objects in the room experience a buzz of excitement. Perhaps one of them will receive their master's attention, if even only for an instant. The master sits upon the green chair and sighs. "Must be another sad love song", the chair thinks to itself. The razor, on the other hand says, "I think he's angry at the world, I hope he's not as angry as that 'Masters of war' song... You know, the one that goes:

And I hope that you die
And you're death'll come soon
I will follow your casket
In the pale afternoon
And I'll watch while you're lowered
Down to your deathbed
And I'll stand o'er your grave
'Til I'm sure that you're dead

The master grabs the yellow notebook and begins jotting down a few lines. The guitar waits patiently, for it knows that the master always uses him and the notebook together. As plain as bread and
---
butter and as sweet as peanut butter and jelly. After a little while, just like clockwork, the notebook is set
aside and the inevitable happens. A quick tuning and he's off. "What'd he write, can you see?" asks the
guitar, even though he'll be one of the first ones to hear. To which the notebook responds, "It's kinda hard
to see considering everything's upside down but it looks like it says..." At that very instance the master
begins strumming along and starts singing softly:

Close your eyes, close the door
You don't have to worry any more.
I'll be your baby tonight.

"Boy, were we off!" shouts the guitar, over the loud playing. "Sounds like a happy song."
After a quick cigarette and a half of joint the master begins to think to himself. He wonders to
himself if all of the pain and sacrifice of all his endless nights of writing and playing are worth
it. He wonders what will fill the next blank page. He remembers the night he turned heads as his audience
watched (some in anger that he "sold out" and others in enjoyment) as he magically blended folk and
rock into one. He remembers the boos, the cheers, and all the fans over the years. A smile is brought to
his face as he thinks of going from playing in corner coffee shops in New York all the way to the big time.
He thinks of the night in the Chelsea Hotel writing "Sad-eyed Lady of the lowlands" for his wife Sarah.
The master sits back in his chair, puts his feet on the table and stares at his pen. He stares deliberately at
his pen as if looking for inspiration. The pens screams out inaudibly, "I love you, man!" But alas. The
master cannot hear these words of love, though, he just continues staring at the pen.
The master then begins thinking about his almost fateful motorcycle crash and begins humming
something about "knocking on heaven's door". The old, rusty razor yells with pride, "He used me that
night, my God! I didn't sleep for a week!" The notebook, always of good humor, responds, "HELL, you
could have killed him right there!" The master is always the center of attention in this room, as you might
expect. Of course, being the greatest of all time can have that effect on people, er... things.
As the master was about to take a little rest he began to pick up a magazine in which he has been
quoted. He ponders the ups and downs of being famous and all of the expectations that come with it. He
---
reads his dialogue from an article about him, "You can't try to come up with songs that people will think
is all hip and cool, you have to write for yourself. There are too many phonies out there and all the one hit
wonders. They come up with a gimmick catch phrase, write some mumbo jumbo and the people love it.
Six months later they've blown all their dough and the fans never even knew who they were."
As he gazes out the window at the pouring rain out side the master wonders again who exactly he is
writing for, who are the ones who really enjoy his work. He doesn't realize that his biggest fan is sitting
right here in this room, it is actually his guitar. The two make a marvelous pair, not unlike the guitar and
the notebook.
Sometimes in this world in which we live in things are not always what they seem. This is the
reason that the master continues with his work- to explain the unseen, to show what is right, what is pure
and true and consequentially, what is wrong and needs to be changed. So with his aging face, fading voice
and wearing guitar he carries on with no direction home, like a rolling stone. He knows how it feels to
have to seek shelter from the storm. He is aware that the times they are a'changing and he's spreading the
word to the uninformed. With that thought he begins to sing a few verses from one of his songs:

Stake my future on a hell of a past

Looks like tomorrow is coming on fast

Ain't complainin' 'bout what I got

Seen better times but who has not....

The guitar understands the master's thoughts as they have been partners for many years. If not for
anyone else, he has been touched by their many nights together. The guitar has experienced what life
outside the room is like through the master's music and is happy inside the dry, warm room. For the master
has predicted that a hard rain's gonna fall and when you're made of wood you can't really hold an umbrella
can you?
As the master is getting ready to lay down for a night's rest he happens to realize that he was
sitting on one of his albums: SELF PORTRAIT by Bob Dylan. And on that note he falls asleep contently
remembering what someone once said to him, "Don't think twice, it's alright."

am at the Tweeter Center in Mansfield, Mass. I'm three hours early. Half of the 
original members of The Who are now part of the house band in Heaven, but on

He made this fat kid look like Joe &#*^@@$$ Montana out on that asphalt war zone where on one side the faded yellow parking lot line was deemed touchdown land and on the opposite side the corroded, and often, sharp chain link fence electrocuted the members of the scored upon team. This was our "frozen tundra of Lambeau Field" (GreenBay Packer's Stadium). I was the QB and the coach and he was the star athlete with a sprinter's speed. We seemed to be missing puzzle pieces to each other's strengths and weaknesses. The best way to describe it is to imagine

a Superman's logo severed in half. Together we were absolutely invincible. The fact that my dysfunctional family was a little more stable than his dysfunctional family (his dad drank cheap hard stuff but my dad only smoked pot) dictated that we spent the majority of the sleepovers over my house- be it Salem, Lynnfield or Swampscott.

Trying to sum up the career of singer/songwriter Bob Dylan in a mere five
page paper is akin to naming all the songs he wrote in alphabetical order- from
“A Fool Such as I” to “You’re no Good.” All anyone has to know is that he has
thirty-three songs that start with W; Need I say more?

Bob Dylan was born Robert Allen Zimmerman on May 24, 1941 in Deluth,
Minnesota. Robert Zimmerman strolled on the stage in the early sixties with a
guitar on his shoulder and a harmonica in his mouth. Music has never been the
same since. He arrived in New York city hoping to replicate his hero, folk singer
Woody Guthrie. Not only did he replicate him but he surpassed him. Dylan’s
writing ability and overall talent quickly propelled him towards stardom and
legend status among the music world.

Dylan is credited with blending folk music with rock and roll and also
reconnecting country and rock. Not to mention as well as reinventing the singer
and songwriter genre. In 1964, Dylan wrote “Mr. Tambourine Man,” which was
the first hit of the Byrds in 1965. And so began folk rock.

The intensity of his performances and his live in-the-studio albums
(Highway 61 Revisited and Blonde on Blonde) were a revelation. His lyrics were
analyzed, debated and quoted like no pop music before them. “I consider myself
a poet first and a musician second. I live like a poet and I’ll die like a poet.” -
Dylan said in 1978 according to “If There’s An Original Thought Out There I
Could Use It Right Now: The Folk Roots of Bob Dylan (Zuckerman). He enlarged

pop's range, as well as its vocabulary. The music Dylan made in 1965 and 1966
revolutionized rock.

His songs electrified the civil rights movement, and breathed new life into
the folk music genre. As the mood in society and music changed so did Dylan as
he altered his perceptions of who he was and what he wanted to say. Dylan has
gone through a variety of stages in his music career but the only label that can
truly be applied is a pioneer.

I think that Dylan has already given so much of himself and so altered the
course of poetics in America that no matter what he does it's just gravy at
this point. Dylan has almost single-handedly brought language back into
its original poetic form which is minstrelsy.

exactly what they were searching for, yet many things were ruled out along the

adults of the '60's and Dylan was a pioneer for this movement. The voice of

A Hard Rain's Gonna Fall

The smoke from a half lit cigarette waves aimlessly through the air. A light brown guitar sits in the corner awaiting the delicate touch of its master. Three empty notebooks sit atop the table curiously wondering what will fill their blank pages. Will there be small sketches of beautiful young women or perhaps some silly verses about how everybody must get stoned? An old weathered, green chair, still feeling the pain of a dropped cigarette, reminices about the time it's owner, the master, once sat for what seemed like an eternity trying to capture the soul of a man named Hollis Brown. An old, rusty razor lays, forgotten, in a corner clutching on to one last piece of cocaine. A broken guitar string sits beneath a pile of trash still humming the melody of what it prays comes true in "Forever Young", and in the state of mind that it will never be thrown away.

A familiar face appears from behind a closed door. All of the objects in the room experience a buzz of excitement. Perhaps one of them will receive their master's attention, if even only for an instant. The master sits upon the green chair and sighs. "Must be another sad love song", the chair thinks to itself. The razor, on the other hand says, "I think he's angry at the world, I hope he's not as angry as that 'Masters of war' song...You know, the one that goes:

And I hope that you die
And you're death'll come soon
I will follow your casket
In the pale afternoon
And I'll watch while you're lowered
Down to your deathbed
And I'll stand o'er your grave
'Til I'm sure that you're dead

The master grabs the yellow notebook and begins jotting down a few lines. The guitar waits patiently, for it knows that the master always uses him and the notebook together. As plain as bread and butter and as sweet as peanut butter and jelly. After a little while, just like clockwork, the notebook is set aside and the inevitable happens. A quick tuning and he's off. "What'd he write, can you see?" asks the guitar, even though he'll be one of the first ones to hear. To which the notebook responds, "It's kinda hard to see considering everything's upside down but it looks like it says..." At that very instance the master begins strumming along and starts singing softly:
---
Close your eyes, close the door
You don't have to worry any more.
I'll be your baby tonight.

"Boy, were we off!" shouts the guitar, over the loud playing. "Sounds like a happy song."

After a quick cigarette and a half of joint the master begins to think to himself. He wonders to himself if all of the pain and sacrifice of all his endless nights of writing and playing are worth it. He wonders what will fill the next blank page. He remembers the night he turned heads as his audience watched (some in anger that he "sold out" and others in enjoyment) as he magically blended folk and rock into one. He remembers the boos, the cheers, and all the fans over the years. A smile is brought to his face as he thinks of going from playing in corner coffee shops in New York all the way to the big time.

He thinks of the night in the Chelsea Hotel writing "Sad-eyed Lady of the lowlands" for his wife Sarah. The master sits back in his chair, puts his feet on the table and stares at his pen. He stares deliberately at his pen as if looking for inspiration. The pens screams out inaudibly, "I love you, man!" But alas. The master cannot hear these words of love, though, he just continues staring at the pen.

The master then begins thinking about his almost fateful motorcycle crash and begins humming something about "knocking on heaven's door". The old, rusty razor yells with pride, "He used me that night, my God! I didn't sleep for a week!" The notebook, always of good humor, responds, "HELL, you could have killed him right there!" The master is always the center of attention in this room, as you might expect. Of course, being the greatest of all time can have that effect on people, er... things.

As the master was about to take a little rest he began to pick up a magazine in which he has been quoted. He ponders the ups and downs of being famous and all of the expectations that come with it. He reads his dialogue from an article about him, "You can't try you have to write for yourself. There are too many phonies out there and all the one hit wonders. They come up with a gimmick catch phrase, write some mumbo jumbo and the people love it. Six months later they've blown all their dough and the fans never even knew who
---
they were."

As he gazes out the window at the pouring rain out side the master wonders again who exactly he is writing for, who are the ones who really enjoy his work. He doesn't realize that his biggest fan is sitting right here in this room, it is actually his guitar. The two make a marvelous pair, not unlike the guitar and the notebook. Sometimes in this world in which we live in things are not always what they seem. This is the reason that the master continues with his work- to explain the unseen, to show what is right, what is pure and true and consequentially, what is wrong and needs to be changed. So with his aging face, fading voice and wearing guitar he carries on with no direction home, like a rolling stone. He knows how it feels to have to seek shelter from the storm. He is aware that the times they are a'changing and he's spreading the word to the uninformed. With that thought he begins to sing a few verses from one of his songs:

Stake my future on a hell of a past
Looks like tomorrow is coming on fast
Ain't complainin' 'bout what I got
Seen better times but who has not....

The guitar understands the master's thoughts as they have been partners for many years. If not for anyone else, he has been touched by their many nights together. The guitar has experienced what life outside the room is like through the master's music and is happy inside the dry, warm room. For the master has predicted that a hard rain's gonna fall and when you're made of wood you can't really hold an umbrella can you?

As the master is getting ready to lay down for a night's rest he happens to realize that he was sitting on one of his albums: SELF PORTRAIT by Bob Dylan. And on that note he falls asleep contently remembering what someone once said to him, "Don't think twice, it's alright."

Connection to

Friedrich Nietzsche once wrote, “The individual has always had to struggle to 
keep from being overwhelmed by the tribe. If you try it, you will be lonely often, and 
sometimes frightened. But no price is too high to pay for the privilege of owning 
yourself.”

At the risk of being guilty of the heresy of paraphrase, I do not think that even Mr.
Bob Dylan himself would argue that his intentions in the creation of his illuminating song 
entitled, “It’s Alright Ma (I’m Only Bleeding),” were to emphasize the importance of 
individualism while rejecting the herd mentality so prevalent in American culture. This 
piece has clearly didactic intentions. But this critique is not concerned with the author’s 
intentions, nor is it interested in giving a history lesson on 1965, the year this song was 
first heard. And for that matter, there will be no talk of hippies or crew cuts, 

The title: “It’s Alright Ma (I’m Only Bleeding)” represents the ultimate form of 
individualism and also acts as one of the motifs that help unite this piece. Your average 
person would probably name this song: I’m in trouble ma (get me to the hospital, 
QUICK!). Hence the title further emphasizes the fact that individualism is the key to 
freedom from the ‘rat race’ that is society, or rather, the collective herd mentality of 
society. Two motifs are present throughout this poem – the first concerns itself with 
overcoming the herd mentality and seeking to find one’s own individuality – and the 
second motif deals with the ambiguous idea of the eclipse, both literally and figuratively, 
in the sense that what is truly important is being forsaken for something that is not. These
---
tensions run parallel and begin to blend into one another: thus validating the achieved
context of the text. The third motif can be found in the five refrains to ‘Ma.’

For them that must obey authority
That they do not respect in any degree
Who despise their jobs, their destinies 13
Speak jealously of them that are free
Cultivate their flowers to be
Nothing more than something
They invest in.

The thirteenth stanza reflects the herd mentality of them. Them refers to those
people who have bought into the idea of commercialism (or a false god) and have ceased
to find the proper place in their life for aesthetics and other “non-profitable” (as far as
material worth) ideologies. The concept of art has been lost to this collective group.
Dylan uses this allegory of cultivating their flowers to illustrate how the simple beauty of
a flower is surpassed by the thought of personal gain and the accumulation of wealth.
These people, or them, would choose to cultivate an entire field of magnificent flowers in
the name of the mighty dollar rather than enjoy them in their natural state. They have
become jealous of the person who can appreciate the natural aesthetics of things in the
world without manipulating them for some type of personal or material gain. A flower
remains free in its natural state. Free and pleasing to the senses. Once it has been
separated from the root, a flower will die. Perhaps if art is commercialized it too will die.

YEAH BY Tom Jensen

"When you find that one thing in life that really grabs you - go with it.
Considering the fact that we all spend the majority of our life either working or
sleeping, doing what you love makes life worth living. It's when the little voice in
your head says 'YeahF that's when you'll know." These few sentences have
been etched into the frame of my existence ever since I sat in Professor
Millman's classroom eight months ago. To hear the magic of these words at the
time they were spoken still awes me - so simple, yet I never realized how
important this concept was. I finally understood how important doing what you
love is. This is the one time in my life where everything fit perfectly together all at
the same time. I was in a class about creative writing being guest lectured by the
novelist who uttered those special words. The author, Deborah Sand, was
obviously grabbed as she has authored many novels and articles on many
subjects. She seemed so happy. A happiness I thought could only be seen in
dreams. What can I say? I was grabbed too.

Throughout my writing life I had always been hindered by rules. As a young
child my writing activities were limited to what I did on my summer vacation and
book reports. As high school came my imagination widened but the spectrum by
which I could showcase my talents didn't - more book reports. Essays comparing
and contrasting two authors' writing styles (I still am haunted by nightmares
regarding two particular authors named Rose and Sizer) were as creative as I
was allowed to get. Even the marvelous institution known as Salem State
College would not free me from my shackles as they required my attendance in
English Composition I. Even though my GPA appreciated the course, the
monotony of writing the same five-paragraph essays lulled my creative senses to
sleep. My love of writing began to fade.

In hopes of rekindling the fire that burned in my pen and my heart, I began
writing on my own. I began writing about anything I could think of: poetry, songs,
even articles for the college newspaper. I soon found that in writing poetry my
creative nature excelled; every rule was thrown away I escaped from form and
structure - there were no commas or paragraphs, no thesises or periods - only
freedom Song writing became my own form of rebellion for all the picky papers 1
---
usually consisted of six members. Each new composition I wrote had a 
guaranteed audience, which both inspired me to write to the best of my ability 
and also worried me about whether or not they would like it. I imagined that 
every writer felt these butterflies and I eventually assured myself that it was 
actually a good thing. For the first time in my academic career, I cared more 
about my peers reactions than I did my teacher's. I craved acceptance as a good 
writer from the majority rather than the one person at the top of the proverbial 
ladder.

My newfound audience became my inspiration for writing papers. I tried to 
blend my creative "anything can come out of this kid's brain" style with my 
trademark sense of humor in an attempt to entertain the reader. I couldn't wait to 
get home to write, be it for class or myself, and I even brought a tiny notebook 
with me to work in case I had any earth-shattering ideas. My inner voice began 
screaming "YEAH!" and for the first time in my life I really did know what I wanted 
to be when I grew up. Inspiration had come over me like it never had before.

Bob Dylan is a writer who I admire most. He was a key spokesman for his 
generation during a time where new ideas were attempting to displace old ones. 
A time when values were changing and differing opinions between father and 
son and mother and daughter were too far apart to bridge the gap. Dylan 
captured an era through his poetry and songs. Dylan's ability to capture the soul 
of so many characters from so many walks of life captivate me to the point where 
he's achieved hero status His writing capability is so above his peers that I could 
only dream of achieving merely half of his status. In my eyes, Bob Dylan is to my 
song-writing and poetry as the peer group (a.k.a. my audience) was to my paper 
writing. His works motivate me to attempt to reach his overall achievements just 
as my audience motivates me to write to their approval and exceed their 
expectations. But the way I see it, my best song is better than Bob s worst and 
that means a lot to me. A struggling young writer must look for inspiration 
anywhere it can be found.

While on the subject of Inspiration, the fact that the creative writing professor 
called me a born writer has further cemented my belief that I can make it in such 
a competitive field. A writer's goal is positive feedback from the reader My
---
teacher's comments, my grandmother crying upon reading a sad poem of mine, and what I feel in my heart about my talent continually motivate me every morning as I awake to be the best. Well, second to Dylan isn't all that bad, is it?

If I was a religious man I'd pray for the day when I can wake up in the morning and be a writer - first and foremost, rather than a painter or landscaper. To be able to push a pencil rather than a paintbrush. I often wonder what wonderful compositions have been lost due to the fact that I have to work a job with my hands rather than my brains. I have not found a job doing what I love yet but at least I know that I'll know it when I see it. Until I catch my break all I can do is dream towards the day when writing is my job rather than just my favorite hobby. But that day will come because echoing in my ear is the word "Yeah!"

As the slow and steady rain falls from the sky down onto the ground I am awakened by the aroma of my father's coffee as it slowly seeps beneath my door and finally reaches my nose. Upon waking and gathering my senses another thought fills my head. If the morning coffee is ready it must be time for my waking routine of having a cup of hot Java in one hand (with cream and sugar, of course) and a newly lit cigarette in the other. My life is just a series of routine after routine. It is my belief that each person's series of routines either makes or breaks their life, and makes up their lifestyle.

We are all creatures of habit, whether we like it or not. My unfortunate luck is that I always seem to get stuck with the bad habits rather than the good ones. You see, a majority of my bad habits, or routines, are all interconnected. Imagine a chain link fence or perhaps a sweater, each individual fabric or link holds all the others in place. Even if one or two individual structures are removed the form, or routine, will remain the same. This interconnectedness is what makes the structure, in my case the routine, the same. The coffee leads to a cigarette and. the cigarette leads to an even greater evil: drugs and alcohol.

My dilemma is that to take only a part out will not change the structure and therefore do no good. There will still be links to the past. With links to the past still remaining it becomes much harder to change a daily pattern. Not only must the chain link fence be disassembled but its very foundation be torn from the ground. It takes a very strong man to do that - to completely change a lifestyle. In order to achieve a goal of this magnitude the right substitutes must be chosen and a new foundation must be poured. School is that substitute and my strength is beginning to build.

Disease of Alcoholism

During my last rehab stint I was told that 20% of the beer drinkers buy 80% of the beer. If you were to compare beer with money in a typical class of twenty students then the numbers will scare you. The statistics are based on the average salary being $50 thousand dollars a year. That means that four of the students would make 200 grand a year and the remaining sixteen would make less than 13 thousand a year.

4 - $200 K
16- $13 K

Now that is a ridiculous figure. Wars have been fought over such inequalities.

With this in mind, what is being done to fight alcoholism? Actually, what can be done to fight alcoholism? One can never escape it. Almost every street corner offers at least one place that serves liquid escape. Bars, Restaurants, Liquor stores, Convenience stores, friend's houses, NyQuil in bathroom vanities, Rum Cake, baseball games, New Years, Christmas, Friday nights, Saturday nights, the list goes on for miles. Unlike many other diseases, alcoholism is not only a physical dependency but a mental one as well. Drink too much and your body becomes dependent. Stop drinking after a long period of abuse and your body will shake. The more you drink the more you need and the more your body learns to hold alcohol. The more you drink the more damage you do to your body.

Alcohol has two societal reasons why it is so powerful. It is both socially acceptable and also cheap. While many drugs are expensive and illegal, you can get a legal buzz for about four dollars. Want to get drunk? How about six bucks for a twelve pack of cheap beer. They make some really cheap Vodka as well. In today's world we are all taught to always put your good face on. We learn to hold back our true selves in an effort to appeal more to people around us. We always desire to be ourselves and to lose our inhibitions. Many people are deadly quiet and shy when sober. Always being afraid to say the wrong thing and scare people away. Alcohol takes away the shyness and allows us to feel free for a time. Many people who suffer from alcoholism wish to prolong that time. Friday nights of going out and reducing stress turn into Wednesday nights of drinking alone after a stressful day of work. The cycle can become so prevalent that one may need to drink in the morning just to start their day.

Treatment is becoming increasing less taboo as more and more high profile people are going into rehabilitation for their disease. Alcoholic's
---
Anonymous can be found all around the world and there are chapters open in almost every city and town. New pills are becoming available in the medical field which make alcoholics very sick when they drink. Many families attempt to help family members suffering from this disease and there are programs and groups available to those in need. In the end, though, the ultimate guide to recovery lies within one's own will power and desire to be healed.
