2

Marijuana has been used as an agent for achieving euphoria since
ancient times; it was described in a Chinese medical compendium traditionally
considered to date from 2737 B.C. This was documented by Chinese emperor
Shen Nung and the focus was on its powers as a medication for rheumatism,
gout, malaria, and oddly enough, absent-mindedness. Mention was made of the
intoxicating properties, but the medicinal values were considered more
important. Its use spread from China to India and then to North Africa and
reached Europe at least as early as 500 A.D. As time passed, the recreational
use of marijuana became much more predominant. (1)

In 1545 the Spanish brought marijuana to the New World. The English
introduced it to Jamestown in 1611 where it became a major commercial crop
alongside tobacco and was often ground and used as a source of fiber. By 1890,
hemp had been replaced by cotton as a major cash crop in the southern states.
Some patent medicines during this time contained marijuana, yet only a small
percentage as those which contained opium or cocaine. It wasn’t until the 1920’s
that marijuana really began to catch on. Some historians state the reason was
prohibition. Its recreational use was restricted to jazz musicians and people in
show biz. “Reefer songs” became the rage of the jazz world and marijuana clubs
sprang up in every major city. Marijuana establishments were tolerated by
authorities because marijuana was not illegal and patrons showed no evidence
of making a nuisance of themselves or disturbing the community.
---
3
Marijuana use as an intoxicant was also commonplace since the 1850's.
A campaign conducted in the 1930's by the Federal Bureau of Narcotics sought
to portray marijuana as a powerful, addictive substance that would lead users
into narcotics addiction. It is still considered a gateway drug by some authorities.
In the 1950's it was an accessory of the beat generation and of course we all
know what happened in the 1960's. The Controlled Substance Act of 1970
classified marijuana, along with heroin and LSD, as a Schedule I drug due to
having the relatively highest abuse potential and no accepted medical use.

Even though the "zero tolerance" climate of the Reagan and Bush
administrations resulted in the passage of strict laws and mandatory sentences
for marijuana possession, marijuana smoking has began another upward trend
since the 1990's, especially among teenagers.

HOW DOES MARIJUANA EFFECT THE BODY?
Some immediate effects of marijuana can include...
■ a faster heartbeat and pulse rate
■ bloodshot eyes
■ dry mouth and throat

HOW DOES MARIJUANA EFFECT YOUR MIND?
■ Studies of marijuana's mental effects show that the drug can impair or reduce
short-term memory
■ can alter sense of time
■ reduce ability to do things which require concentration, swift reactions and
coordination (such as driving a car or studying for Health and Wellness
class)
---
4

Laboratory studies have shown that animals exhibit symptoms of drug
withdrawal after cessation to prolonged marijuana exposure. Some human
studies have also demonstrated withdrawal symptoms such as irritability,
stomach pains, aggression, and anxiety after stopping using cannabis. George
Koob, an addiction researcher from the Scripps Research Institute on La Jolla,
California, claims the new message from animals is simple: "The more we
discover about the neurobiology of addiction the more common elements we're
seeing between THC (cannabis' active ingredient) and other drugs of abuse.
And for Koob, one of these newly discovered "common elements" is marijuana's
ability to trigger chemical changes in the brain that lead to strong withdrawal
symptoms. (2)

In humans, some researchers claim to see clear evidence of insomnia,
anxiety, and even flu-like symptoms in heavy cannabis users who abstain. But if
there is a consensus, it is that the symptoms are mild and variable. By contrast,
Koob's rats are shivering wrecks. Does this mean that marijuana is more
addictive than we think? Another debate rages over animal studies into the
short-term effects of marijuana on brain chemistry. Heroin, cocaine, alcohol and
nicotine all trigger a surge in the chemical dopamine in a small midbrain
structure called the nucleus accumbens. Many researchers regard this as a
hallmark of an addictive substance. Last year, experiments showed that
cannabis presses the same dopamine button in rats, leading to claims that the
---
5

drug must be more addictive than previously thought. To critics, it is just another
example of those old exaggerated fears.

What nobody tells you, says John Morgan, a pharmacologist at City
University of New York Medical School, is that rats don't like cannabis. It is easy
for them to get hooked on heroine or cocaine—but not marijuana. Nor, Morgan
claims, are researchers exactly open about awkward observations, such as the
fact that there are plenty of non-addictive drugs that stimulate dopamine in
the brain. It is easy to understand why biologists want to find simple chemical
traits that are shared by all addictive drugs. Unfortunately, the differences are as
important as the similarities when it comes to weighing the relative risks and
pleasures involved in using drugs. And subjectively, at least, the intense rush of
cocaine and orgasm-like high of heroin have little in common with marijuana's
subtler effects. Amid all of the research that has been studied, the obvious fact is
that marijuana use is still safer than heroin, cocaine and alcohol abuse. In the
giant Totem Pole of narcotics, marijuana is still the closest to the ground. (3)
---
6

(2) ADDICTION LETTER August 1995, Volume 11 Issue 8 page 1-2
(3) THE NEW SCIENTIST October 28, 200 pages 15-18

There is no single factor that either makes or breaks addiction or sobriety. Everything in this world is part of one giant chain reaction. Just as the earth rotates on its axis and revolves around the sun, one’s life and patterns are often one giant circle of repetition. You wake up you take a shower, you brush your teeth, you have breakfast and go to work. You come home and have dinner, watch TV, pick out your clothes for the coming day and go to sleep. The next morning the cycle continues. We are all taught repetition as we are young and we are conditioned to it. Hence the struggles of an addict. This cycle becomes ingrained into the fabric of your existence. You hang with the same friends and you do the same things. You drink the same beer, you do the same drugs. You spend the same money. The whirlwind in which you're caught in moves so fast and the suction becomes so strong that you can not expect to take out just one variable of the equation and immediately begin a new pattern of existence. In the case of the addict you must make changes so drastic as to knock the rotation off its axis and into a new one.

I have two schools of thought on fighting drug addiction and alcoholism. The first one is to realize the biggest evils you face and substitute a lesser for the worse ones. The methadone program for heroin addicts. In terms of my father, going from raging alcoholic to a pot smoker. He lives a functional life by smoking dope at night. If he still drank then he would be dead. He substituted the apple for an orange. This may cure the specific addiction yet it does not change your addictive nature. He now only stutters and forgets his name occasionally. Rather than forgetting whole weeks and weekends due to alcohol induced blackouts he might now only forget to check his mail. Does this work? Yes, to a degree. He has the will power to stick to the plan. I consider this idea a compromise where you don't get exactly what you want but you still get what you need.

My other school of though on addiction is to use all types of drugs and alcohol yet only on a limited basis therefor limiting the effects of excessive use of any one drink or drug. For instance, Monday night smoke a little dope. Tuesday night maybe a few painkillers, Wednesday night snort a few lines, Thursday night have a few beers and so forth. By using this system you do not get the constant nosebleeds, hangovers or memory losses that would occur if you concentrated your addiction in one specific area. You are still an addict but I think that many addicts would live longer lives if they practiced this philosophy. Still you run the risk of overcoming a multitude of addictions when you finally come to the point where you really want to quit. I have tried both of these schools of thought and am perhaps the originator of this way of thinking. Both of these have their positives and negatives anyway you look at it.
---
I often ponder the possibility of knocking my addictive habits off their axis by completely changing my surroundings. I have an aunt in Florida who is dying for me to come down and live with her. Her husband is an alcoholic but he's done real well over the last few months. He works out of state in order to attempt to save their marriage and she is dying for companionship. My life is very entrenched in Salem and so is my addiction. I see familiar memories, faces and past party spots on a daily basis. My family needs me here and my schooling is going phenomenally well as I have made Dean's List for five semesters in a row. I'm making great money working with great people at my job and having lost my license for another year and a half the bus here really comes in handy. But often in the back of my mind I have thought that leaving might be the best solution. A change as big as moving a thousand miles away is the type needed when trying to overcome an addiction such as mine. But even this is not a surefire way to break the chain.

Go ahead and try

Go ahead and try
Go ahead and try

I know what I must do. I must confine myself to isolation and dive into my own pool of knowledge. I must dedicate myself to sobriety and all of its positive and negative ramifications. I will lose something in the process but I will also gain from it. I know that I will do something great in this world as long as I do not die from an overdose or drunk driving accident ( I've had two already and my first one brought me within three inches to the left of a telephone pole of death). My fate is in my hands and only my hands. Excuses are like assholes... everybody's got one. I know at one end of the road there is a light at the end of the tunnel and at the other end a dead end. The choice is mine.

What is wellness? That is certainly a good question to start with when one is trying to decide how well one's well is. I would consider wellness the successful achievement of one limiting one's negative characteristics and traits. By limiting the negative in one's collective body and soul the effect, therefore, is accenting the positive. Addition by subtraction if you will. So, since coming to the very real acceptance of who I am and what I do I am able to make a judgment over how well is my wellness. What flaws have been noticed, studied, and fixed? What traits have I stepped back from my eyes and observed from another frame of reference? How have I felt about my relationships with friends and family? What have I yet to achieve on the Totem Pole of life, how far have I climbed? All things of this nature make for interesting talk and type but the main element one has to remember is that all of these subjects are subjective to the observer. Anyone may relate oneself to others in an attempt to compare actions and sometimes even justify an unjust act. One's immediate circle acts as the shell in which the egg is kept. On one hand, the shell can protect the egg from predators, harm and frying pans but the shell also succeeds in limiting how far the egg can expand and thereby cut off the egg from the far away chicken of happiness. I am the egg man, sorry Mr. Lennon.

But, as the more I learn the more I see how correct my poetry can be. It seems society has reached the point where it can no longer envision evil and therefore attempt to prevent evil from happening in the first place. It is only after
---
the original act has been done that the necessary corrections are deemed
worthy.

Cannot fix the flaw - only patch the hole
The potential of diamonds results in coal
Able to race the race though blind to the goal
Only glimpses and pieces never the whole

I am living the paradox which is the same as society. I am able to see the goal
ahead of me. I am well aware of my major flaws and I certainly do hold the
potential for greatness and diamonds. That is the good part. The problem lies in
the fact that I am aware of the flaw but I choose to only patch the hole. Never
giant changes, only small subtleties which meagerly reshape my path towards
the future. The dark side of the diamond shows his grim face. In life, knowledge
is the ultimate power but how should one feel if he is the knower yet not the
doer? So many ignorant fools would die to think just one great thought. Why take
it for granted when one has so much to share in so little time? This is the
dilemma of the people caught in the trap.

My wellness is as it finds me, finds me as I have been, in the same
structure, same form. Faces change just as does the weather. My feet are
always moving but it’s not always up. A life which was created and I now call my
own. A time when the only time one can truly take the time to gather one’s inner
---
thoughts is a time when is only an afterthought. A busy productive day only ends in an even busier unproductive night. Voices have warned me and wisdom has guided these voices. The face has a name and the deed is a game. Just as the earth spins so does a day as patterns emerge and it takes more to wash away a sand castle than just a single wave. Or so the saying goes...

WHAT_IT_IS: Printed text on standard white paper.

MARIJUANA ADDICTION

Tom Jensen
Wealth and Hellness ☺
April 18, 2001
---
2
Marijuana has been used as an agent for achieving euphoria since
ancient times; it was described in a Chinese medical compendium traditionally
considered to date from 2737 B.C. This was documented by Chinese emperor
Shen Nung and the focus was on its powers as a medication for rheumatism,
gout, malaria, and oddly enough, absent-mindedness. Mention was made of the
intoxicating properties, but the medicinal values were considered more
important. Its use spread from China to India and then to North Africa and
reached Europe at least as early as 500 A.D. As time passed, the recreational
use of marijuana became much more predominant. (1)

In 1545 the Spanish brought marijuana to the New World. The English
introduced it to Jamestown in 1611 where it became a major commercial crop
alongside tobacco and was often ground and used as a source of fiber. By 1890,
hemp had been replaced by cotton as a major cash crop in the southern states.
Some patent medicines during this time contained marijuana, yet only a small
percentage as those which contained opium or cocaine. It wasn't until the 1920's
that marijuana really began to catch on. Some historians state the reason was
that recreational use was restricted to jazz musicians and people in
prohibition. Its “Reefer songs” became the rage of the jazz world and marijuana clubs
sprang up in every major city. Marijuana establishments were tolerated by
authorities because marijuana was not illegal and patrons showed no evidence
of making a nuisance of themselves or disturbing the community.
---
3
Marijuana use as an intoxicant was also commonplace since the 1850's.
A campaign conducted in the 1930's by the Federal Bureau of Narcotics sought
to portray marijuana as a powerful, addictive substance that would lead users
into narcotics addiction. It is still considered a gateway drug by some authorities.
In the 1950's it was an accessory of the beat generation and of course we all
know what happened in the 1960's. The Controlled Substance Act of 1970
classified marijuana, along with heroin and LSD, as a Schedule I drug due to
having the relatively highest abuse potential and no accepted medical use.

Even though the “zero tolerance” climate of the Reagan and Bush
administrations resulted in the passage of strict laws and mandatory sentences
for marijuana possession, marijuana smoking has began another upward trend
since the 1990's, especially among teenagers.

HOW DOES MARIJUANA EFFECT THE BODY?
Some immediate effects of marijuana can include...
■ a faster heartbeat and pulse rate
■ bloodshot eyes
■ dry mouth and throat

HOW DOES MARIJUANA EFFECT YOUR MIND?
Studies of marijuana's mental effects show that the drug can impair or reduce
short-term memory
■ can alter sense of time
■ reduce ability to do things which require concentration, swift reactions and
coordination (such as driving a car or studying for Health and Wellness class)
---
4

Laboratory studies have shown that animals exhibit symptoms of drug
withdrawal after cessation to prolonged marijuana exposure. Some human
studies have also demonstrated withdrawal symptoms such as irritability,
stomach pains, aggression, and anxiety after stopping using cannabis. George
Koob, an addiction researcher from the Scripps Research Institute on La Jolla,
California, claims the new message from animals is simple: “The more we
discover about the neurobiology of addiction the more common elements we're
seeing between THC (cannabis’ active ingredient) and other drugs of abuse. And
for Koob, one of these newly discovered “common elements” is marijuana’s
ability to trigger chemical changes in the brain that lead to strong withdrawal
symptoms. (2)

In humans, some researchers claim to see clear evidence of insomnia,
anxiety, and even flu-like symptoms in heavy cannabis users who abstain. But if
there is a consensus, it is that the symptoms are mild and variable. By contrast,
Koob’s rats are shivering wrecks. Does this mean that marijuana is more
addictive than we think? Another debate rages over animal studies into the short-
term effects of marijuana on brain chemistry. Heroin, cocaine, alcohol and
nicotine all trigger a surge in the chemical dopamine in a small midbrain structure
called the nucleus accumbens. Many researchers regard this as a hallmark of an
addictive substance. Last year, experiments showed that cannabis presses the
same dopamine button in rats, leading to claims that the drug must be more
---
addictive than previously thought. To critics, it is just another example of those
old exaggerated fears.

What nobody tells you, says John Morgan, a pharmacologist at City
University of New York Medical School, is that rats don't like cannabis. It is easy
for them to get hooked on heroine or cocaine—but not marijuana. Nor, Morgan
claims, are researchers exactly open about awkward observations, such as the
fact that there are plenty of non-addictive drugs that stimulate dopamine in
the brain. It is easy to understand why biologists want to find simple chemical
traits that are shared by all addictive drugs. Unfortunately, the differences are as
important as the similarities when it comes to weighing the relative risks and
pleasures involved in using drugs. And subjectively, at least, the intense rush of
cocaine and orgasm-like high of heroin have little in common with marijuana's
subtler effects. Amid all of the research that has been studied, the obvious fact is
that marijuana use is still safer than heroin, cocaine and alcohol abuse. In the
giant Totem Pole of narcotics, marijuana is still the closest to the ground. (3)

There is no single factor that either makes or breaks addiction or sobriety. Everything in this world is part of one giant chain reaction. Just as the earth rotates on its axis and revolves around the sun one’s life and patterns are often one giant circle of repetition. You wake up you take a shower, you brush your teeth, you have breakfast and go to work. You come home and have dinner, watch TV, pick out your clothes for the coming day and go to sleep. The next morning the cycle continues. We are all taught repetition as we are young and we are conditioned to it. Hence the struggles of an addict. This cycle becomes ingrained into the fabric of your existence. You hang with the same friends and you do the same things. You drink the same beer, you do the same drugs. You spend the same money. The whirlwind in which you’re caught in moves so fast and the suction becomes so strong that you can not expect to take out just one variable of the equation and immediately begin a new pattern of existence. In the case of the addict you must make changes so drastic as to knock the rotation off its axis and into a new one.

I have two schools of thought on fighting drug addiction and alcoholism. The first one is to realize the biggest evils you face and substitute a lesser for the worse ones. The methadone program for heroin addicts. In terms of my father, going from raging alcoholic to a pot smoker. He lives a functional life by smoking dope at night. If he still drank then he would be dead. He substituted the apple for an orange. This may cure the specific addiction yet it does not change your addictive nature. He now only stutters and forgets his name occasionally. Rather than forgetting whole weeks and weekends due to alcohol induced blackouts he might now only forget to check his mail. Does this work? Yes, to a degree. He has the will power to stick to the plan. I consider this idea a compromise where you don’t get exactly what you want but you still get what you need.

My other school of though on addiction is to use all types of drugs and alcohol yet only on a limited basis therefor limiting the effects of excessive use of any one drink or drug. For instance, Monday night smoke a little dope. Tuesday night maybe a few painkillers, Wednesday night snort a few lines, Thursday night have a few beers and so forth. By using this system you do not get the constant nosebleeds, hangovers or memory losses that would occur if you concentrated your addiction in one specific area. You are still an addict but I think that many addicts would live longer lives if they practiced this philosophy. Still you run the risk of overcoming a multitude of addictions when you finally come to the point where you really want to quit. I have tried both of these schools of thought and am perhaps the originator of this way of thinking. Both of these have their positives and negatives anyway you look at it.

I often ponder the possibility of knocking my addictive habits off their axis by completely changing my surroundings. I have an aunt in Florida who is dying for me to come down and live with her. Her husband is an alcoholic but he’s done real well over the last few months. He works out of state in order to attempt

But often in the back of my mind I have thought that leaving might be the best solution. Disease of Alcoholism

During my last rehab stint I was told that 20% of the beer drinkers buy
80% of the beer. If you were to compare beer with money in a typical class of
twenty students then the numbers will scare you. The statistics are based on the
average salary being $50 thousand dollars a year. That means that four of the
students would make 200 grand a year and the remaining sixteen would make
less than 13 thousand a year.

4 - $200 K
16- $13 K

Now that is a ridiculous figure. Wars have been fought over such inequalities.

With this in mind, what is being done to fight alcoholism? Actually, what
can be done to fight alcoholism? One can never escape it. Almost every street
corner offers at least one place that serves liquid escape. Bars, Restaurants,
Liquor stores, Convenience stores, friend’s houses, NyQuil in bathroom vanities,
Rum Cake, baseball games, New Years, Christmas, Friday nights, Saturday
nights, the list goes on for miles. Unlike many other diseases, alcoholism is not
only a physical dependency but a mental one as well. Drink too much and your
body becomes dependent. Stop drinking after a long period of abuse and your
body will shake. The more you drink the more you need and the more your body
learns to hold alcohol. The more you drink the more damage you do to your
body.

Alcohol has two societal reasons why it is so powerful. It is both socially
acceptable and also cheap. While many drugs are expensive and illegal, you
can get a legal buzz for about four dollars. Want to get drunk? How about six
bucks for a twelve pack of cheap beer. They make some really cheap Vodka as
well. In today’s world we are all taught to always put your good face on. We
learn to hold back our true selves in an effort to appeal more to people around
us. We always desire to be ourselves and to lose our inhibitions. Many people
are deadly quiet and shy when sober. Always being afraid to say the wrong thing
and scare people away. Alcohol takes away the shyness and allows us to feel
free for a time. Many people who suffer from alcoholism wish to prolong that
time. Friday nights of going out and reducing stress turn into Wednesday nights
of drinking alone after a stressful day of work. The cycle can become so
prevalent that one may need to drink in the morning just to start their day.

Treatment is becoming increasing less taboo as more and more high
profile people are going into rehabilitation for their disease. Alcoholic’s
---
Anonymous can be found all around the world and there are chapters open in 
almost every city and town. New pills are becoming available in the medical field 
which make alcoholics very sick when they drink. Many families attempt to help 
family members suffering from this disease and there are programs and groups 
available to those in need. In the end, though, the ultimate guide to recovery lies 
within one's own power and desire to be healed.

WORDS:
COPING

Tom Jensen

June 10, 2001

Health and Wellness

That people get sick or experience unpleasant emotions in response to stress should come as no surprise. What may seem more surprising is that most people who experience life crises remain healthy. This resiliency in the face of
---
stress reflects the ways people deal with stressful situations, or ways of coping. 
Many coping strategies are consciously selected, whereas others, known as 
defense mechanisms, are largely unconscious. A study of women hospitalized 
while awaiting biopsies to determine whether or not they had breast cancer 
shows how variable coping responses can be. All thirty women were in the same 
potentially life-threatening situation, but their emotional responses and ability to 
function despite their anxiety varied considerably. One woman denied she had 
problem, blaming the lump on a fall in the bathtub. Another complained that her 
husband, not her, was the one who required medical attention. And still others 
drew on their religious faith to cope with their illness. 

Researchers often distinguish between three types of coping strategies: 
(1) efforts to change the situation, (2) efforts to alter one's cognition about the 
situation, and (3) efforts to alter the unpleasant emotional consequences of 
stress. In other words, if a person cannot change a stressful situation directly, he 
or she may try to change his or her perception of it or the emotion it endangers. 

Efforts to cope by changing the situation typically involve problem solving. 
The individual may try to remove the stressor, plan ways of resolving the 
situation, or seek advice or assistance from others in changing the situation. 
People who are high in problem solving ability and who have a problem - solving 
orientation ( a tendency to define potential problems as challenging and to 
confront them directly) tend to report less stress and fewer psychological
---
symptoms than other subjects. Individuals with a problem-focused orientation
tend to endorse questionnaire statements such as, “I am the kind of person who
takes action rather than just thinks or complains about a situation.

Coping by changing one’s cognition or appraisal of the situation often
involves reframing an event mentally in order to make it seem less threatening.
For example, a person who is anxious about giving a speech may
say to himself, “Come on now, this is ridiculous. You are just talking to a bunch
of people who are interested in what you have to say.” An example of reframing
a more tragic situation is the way a man dying of AIDS combined cognitive
restructuring with a sense of humor: “I made a list of all other diseases I would
rather not have than AIDS: Lou Gehrig’s disease, being in a wheelchair,
rheumatoid arthritis, when you are in knots and in terrible pain. So I said you
have to get some perspective on this, and where you are on the Great Nasty
Disease List.”

A third way people cope with a stressful situation is by trying to relieve the
associated emotional state, as when a person smiles nervously to try to relegate
anxiety. Alcohol and drugs are common mechanisms for escaping emotional
distress, as a distraction. Another AIDS patient, in describing his efforts to cope
with distressing emotions confided, “I used to depend on drugs a lot to change
my mood. Once in awhile, I still find that if I can’t feel better any other way I will
take a puff of grass or a glass of wine, or I use music. There are certain
---
recordings that can really change my mood drastically. I play it loud and I dance
around and try to clear my head.”

Although many of the coping strategies described above are conscious or
could be readily be made conscious if attention were called to them, other
coping strategies, known as defense mechanisms, are unconscious and involve
greater self-deception. Defense mechanisms are unconscious mental processes
aimed at protecting the person from experiencing unpleasant emotions or
bolstering positive affect. The most widely used defense mechanism is
repression, an unconscious mechanism that keeps thoughts or memories that
would be to threatening to acknowledge from awareness. A similar mechanism is
denial, in which the person refuses to acknowledge external realities (such as
having cancer) or emotions (such as anxiety), rather than thoughts. Denial is at
work when someone notices a skin blemish but concludes it’s nothing. Much of
the time it is nothing, but this defense can lead to a lack of treatment or death.

In projection, a person attributes his own unacknowledged feelings or
impulses to others. The hard driving businessman who thinks his competitors,
suppliers and customers are always trying to cheat him may be in fact the one
with questionable ethics. To recognize his own greed and selfishness would
conflict with his conscious, so he sees these traits in others. In reaction
formation, the person turns unacceptable impulses or feelings into their
opposites. For example, at the same time televangelist Jimmy Swaggert was
---
preaching the evils of sex to millions, he was regularly seeing a prostitute. His conscious repulsion towards sexuality, and particularly illicit sexuality, apparently masked a tremendous need for it. 

Sublimation involves converting sexual or aggressive impulses into socially acceptable activities. A young boy may turn his feelings of competition with his father or brother into a desire to excel in competitive sports or achieve a successful business when he gets older. Rationalization means explaining away actions in a seemingly logical way to avoid uncomfortable feelings, especially guilt or shame. A student who plagiarizes her term paper and justifies her actions by saying passing the course will help her public policy degree and serve the community is using rationalization to justify her dishonesty. Passive aggression is the indirect expression of anger towards others. One administrator frustrated everyone around her by 'sitting on' important documents which required a fast turnaround. To be actively aggressive would run afoul of her moral standards and potentially lead to a reprimand from her boss, so she accomplished the same goal - frustrating coworkers and thus satisfying her aggressive impulses - in a way that allowed her to disavow any intention or responsibility.

Just as people tailor their problem-solving efforts to specific situations, so too do people typically use defense mechanisms flexibly and creatively. Using defenses is neither abnormal nor unhealthy. In actuality, some degree of
---
defensive distortion can be useful to the human psyche. Defenses become dysfunctional when they inhibit adaptive functioning rather than foster it.

A Hard Rain's Gonna Fall

The smoke from a half lit cigarette waves aimlessly through the air. A light brown guitar sits in the corner awaiting the delicate touch of its master. Three empty notebooks sit atop the table curiously wondering what will fill their blank pages. Will there be small sketches of beautiful young women or perhaps some silly verses about how everybody must get stoned? An old weathered, green chair, still feeling the pain of a dropped cigarette, reminisces about the time it's owner, the master, once sat for what seemed like an eternity trying to capture the soul of a man named Hollis Brown. An old, rusty razor lays, forgotten, in a corner clutching on to one last piece of cocaine. A broken guitar string sits beneath a pile of trash still humming the melody of what it prays comes true in "Forever Young", and in the state of mind that it will never be thrown away.

A familiar face appears from behind a closed door. All of the objects in the room experience a buzz of excitement. Perhaps one of them will receive their master's attention, if even only for an instant. The master sits upon the green chair and sighs. "Must be another sad love song", the chair thinks to itself. The razor, on the other hand says, "I think he's angry at the world, I hope he's not as angry as that 'Masters of war' song... You know, the one that goes:

And I hope you die
And you're death'll come soon
I will follow your casket
In the pale afternoon
And I'll watch while you're lowered
Down to your deathbed
And I'll stand o'er your grave
'Til I'm sure that you're dead

The master grabs the yellow notebook and begins jotting down a few lines. The guitar waits patiently, for it knows that the master always uses him and the notebook together. As plain as bread and butter and as sweet as peanut butter and jelly. After a little while, just like clockwork, the notebook is set aside and the inevitable happens. A quick tuning and he's off. "What'd he write, can you see?" asks the guitar, even though he'll be one of the first ones to hear. To which the notebook responds, "It's kinda hard to see considering everything's upside down but it looks like it says..." At that very instance the master begins strumming along and starts singing softly:
---
they were."

As he gazes out the window at the pouring rain out side the master wonders again who exactly he is writing for, who are the ones who really enjoy his work. He doesn't realize that his biggest fan is sitting right here in this room, it is actually his guitar. The two make a marvelous pair, not unlike the guitar and the notebook. Sometimes in this world in which we live in things are not always what they seem. This is the reason that the master continues with his work- to explain the unseen, to show what is right, what is pure and true and consequentially, what is wrong and needs to be changed. So with his aging face, fading voice and wearing guitar he carries on with no direction home, like a rolling stone. He knows how it feels to have to seek shelter from the storm. He is aware that the times they are a'changing and he's spreading the word to the uninformed. With that thought he begins to sing a few verses from one of his songs:

Stake my future on a hell of a past
Looks like tomorrow is coming on fast
Ain't complainin' 'bout what I got
Seen better times but who has not....

The guitar understands the master's thoughts as they have been partners for many years. If not for anyone else, he has been touched by their many nights together. The guitar has experienced what life outside the room is like through the master's music and is happy inside the dry, warm room. For the master has predicted that a hard rain's gonna fall and when you're made of wood you can't really hold an umbrella can you?

As the master is getting ready to lay down for a night's rest he happens to realize that he was sitting on one of his albums: SELF PORTRAIT by Bob Dylan. And on that note he falls asleep contently remembering what someone once said to him, "Don't think twice, it's alright."

She sits in the doctor's office watching several children around her playing
with their toys, wondering why life couldn't have been that simple for her. No
limitations, no funny looks - only a carefree child's mentality. It seems that these
children have never knew anything but fitting in and having fun. Of course, she's
older now, and with age comes the responsibility of making it to the doctor's
office by herself. Yet her father still accompanies her and tries his best to
comfort her, hiding his own nervousness. His eyes appear a little weary after a
two-hour drive but important news should not be heard alone.

The nurse calls her name as she wipes her sweaty palm on the sides of
her jeans. Her father follows. This day could be one of the most important of her
life, on par only with high school graduation and almost dying of bacterial
meningitis as a very young child. The latter being the reason why she's in the
doctor's office in the first place. Every parent prays for a perfect child. This visit
could be a step closer to perfection.

Though she survived the bacterial meningitis some of her hearing did not.
Her left ear was diagnosed with moderate hearing loss and her right ear, a mild
hearing loss. At four years old she was fitted for over-the-ear hearing aids.
Childhood had its periods of ups and downs as young children can be cruel and
---
side effects. She's on such a strong dose that when she stops taking if she has 
to be weaned off of if and if she suddenly stopped taking it her heart could stop. 
The prednisone suppresses the immune system to the point where it is at about 
half strength. It is hoped that the immune system is attacking her hearing and 
causing the loss. Stop the immune system and thereby stop the hearing loss. 

Over the last three weeks she has suffered from insomnia, bloating, 
nausea, muscle weakness, head ache and excessive mood swings (just ask her 
boyfriend). She missed several days of school and work after taking the first 
dose of medicine but hopes in the end that it will be well worth the pain. 

This appointment will show how the prednisone has reacted and whether or 
not there is reason to continue treatment. Any signs of her hearing returning will 
warrant more treatment and continued hope. Past doctors have warned her that 
her good ear could possibly follow the same path as her bad ear rendering her 
deaf. A chilling thought for a twenty-year old supposedly in the prime of her life. 

Finally, the doctor enters the room. He greets them both and offers a 
warm smile which brightens both the father and the daughter's faces. He 
proceeds to tell them that he is the bearer of good news. It seems that her bad 
ear has gone up 10 decibels since before treatment She is elated. He also says 
that a new hearing aid can increase her good ear from 70% hearing to roughly 
95% and adds a feature that includes a microphone that her teacher could wear 
that would transmit his voice directly into an attachment to her hearing aid. 
Technology isn't cheap, though, this hearing aid costs about $3,600. 

Doctors say her hearing should improve with time though they predict a 
long process. It took years for her hearing to get this far, and the recovery 
process is expected to be just as long. There is finally hope....

As you walk in, you briefly survey the scene. There are nine or ten students typing away on their keyboards – typing up reports and E-mailing their friends. I believe that the staff of this computer lab makes better signs than anyone I’ve ever met, and a lot of them too. A pretty red one reads “out of order”. Over in the corner is a computer with two nicely crafted works of art “Not working, Sorry” and “Need new power supply”. This is just the beginning. I mentioned the staff’s creativity but I neglected to mention their resourcefulness. Immediately on your right as you walk in you see two computers set aside for the physically challenged (yes, another computer made sign complete with color). If you look closely you’ll see that on one of them the monitor is being held up with two academic computing books. The last time I checked, books were for reading and maybe for holding up the leg of your old broken sofa, not for holding up monitors where someone in a wheelchair might have a hard time getting out of the way if it were to fall. I do admit that it is a resourceful idea, though.

I come into this lab several times a week and don’t get me wrong, the staff here does a wonderful job at working with what they have (which at the moment isn’t much). If you have a problem, and the odds are you will, they always do the best they can. Six out of the twenty-three computers available to the students aren’t functioning correctly. I did the math quickly and it’s a little over one/fourth. Considering this is the most highly used lab on campus I expect a little more than that and I think you do too. One thing that I do like is that they have one clock on each side of the room, that way if I forget which side it’s on and look hastily I’m bound to see one of them. They also have three fans located strategically around the room. It

seems to this untrained eye that a pattern is developing here – what we don't need, they have

She sits in the doctor's office watching several children around her playing
with their toys, wondering why life couldn't have been that simple for her. No
limitations, no funny looks - only a carefree child's mentality. It seems that these
children have never knew anything but fitting in and having fun. Of course, she's
older now, and with age comes the responsibility of making it to the doctor's
office by herself. Yet her father still accompanies her and tries his best to comfort
her, hiding his own nervousness. His eyes appear a little weary after a two-hour
drive but important news should not be heard alone.
The nurse calls her name as she wipes her sweaty palm on the sides of
her jeans. Her father follows. This day could be one of the most important of her
life, on par only with high school graduation and almost dying of bacterial
meningitis as a very young child. The latter being the reason why she's in the
doctor's office in the first place. Every parent prays for a perfect child. This visit
could be a step closer to perfection.
Though she survived the bacterial meningitis some of her hearing did not.
Her left ear was diagnosed with moderate hearing loss and her right ear, a mild
hearing loss. At four years old she was fitted for over-the-ear hearing aids.
Childhood had its periods of ups and downs as young children can be cruel and
outcast what they don't understand. The hearing aids provided some relief in the
classroom but she still suffered additional hearing losses during the coming
years. Second grade is remembered only as an endless series of tests trying to
---
discover what caused yet another hearing loss. Early memories include this seven year old girl being placed in a giant tube and also having ice water placed in her ears.

As a senior in high school more hearing problems occurred. It became increasingly difficult for her to understand lectures in class, and even participate. Quite a burden for a mere teenager to bear. She later admits that she was in complete denial of the fact that her right ear was hearing less and less with each day. She did nothing.

Eventually, she could deny no more. Three years later she has practically no hearing in her right ear, as the left ear remains steady, yet below normal. But an unproven and unapproved treatment has turned countless nights of crying into guarded hope. Hope, which has been long awaited for and comes by the name of prednisone.

Prednisone is a highly controversial drug when used in cases involving hearing loss. It is believed that she suffers from auto-immune inner ear syndrome, though is not yet recognized by the FDA, it is in the process of being tested. The treatment is not covered by any insurance and offers a variety of side effects. She's on such a strong dose that when she stops taking it she has to be weaned off of it and if she suddenly stopped taking it her heart could stop. The prednisone suppresses the immune system to the point where it is at about half strength. It is hoped that the immune system is attacking her hearing and causing the loss. Stop the immune system and thereby stop the hearing loss.
---
Over the last three weeks she has suffered from insomnia, bloating, nausea, muscle weakness, head ache and excessive mood swings (just ask her boyfriend). She missed several days of school and work after taking the first dose of medicine but hopes in the end that it will be well worth the pain.

This appointment will show how the prednisone has reacted and whether or not there is reason to continue treatment. Any signs of her hearing returning that her good ear could possibly follow the same path as her bad ear rendering her deaf. A chilling thought for a twenty-year old supposedly in the prime of her life.

Finally, the doctor enters the room. He greets them both and offers a warm smile which brightens both the father and the daughter's faces. He proceeds to tell them that he is the bearer of good news. It seems that her bad ear has gone up 10 decibels since before treatment. She is elated. He also says that a new hearing aid can increase her good ear from 70% hearing to roughly 95% and adds a feature that includes a microphone that her teacher could wear that would transmit his voice directly into an attachment to her hearing aid. Technology isn't cheap, though, this hearing aid costs about $3,600.

Doctors say her hearing should improve with time though they predict a long process. It took years for her hearing to get this far, and the recovery process is expected to be just as long. There is finally hope....

But while Peter, an English major, was getting hosed off in the shade, Steve was just beginning to run the race a second time. Peter willingly acknowledged the roll that Steve, also 20, played in the race, "He gave me the win. His job was just to go out there and pull me. He's my training partner and he wanted to do another round. He's in a little better shape than I am right now."

Mallett and Meinett are two of the anchors of the cross-country team at UNH and generally run about 70 and 100 miles a week, respectively. Over the summer they try to run together twice a week. Steve Meinett's motivation for the race was not a selfish one,
---
"[I was running] strictly for my buddy. I was helping him out. I told him before that I was going to do it twice. I'm thinking of doing a ten-miler so I wanted to go a little further. I figured I'll help him and then I'll just do it again." This win marks the third time that Mallett, a Manchester, NH native whose aunt lives in Lynnfield, has competed in this race. "Last year I was dehydrated and went out the back door. This year I used it as a tune-up race."

Meinett's selfless act personified a race in which the overall goal is to raise scholarship money for graduating seniors as much as lower finishing times. Meinett, a junior majoring in sociology, enjoyed running in Lynnfield for the first time but admitted that, "the second time was definitely tougher. I was feeling the heat."

As for the women's winner, it was up to Amy Wallace, whose younger bother Shawn had won the race the last two years yet had to sit out this year's with an injury, to defend the family name. With a winning time of 20:10, she did just that. 

Originally from Wakefield, Wallace still had plenty of familiar faces surrounding her during the race, even though her brother was forced to watch from the crowd. "I'm here cheering on these guys. They're my idols," said Shawn, last year's injured winner.

Amy's older brother, Bill Wallace, a science teacher at Lynnfield High School, ran the race while pushing his daughter in a stroller. Amy's mother, Judy, also competed this year and said, "I am very proud of her. I am proud of my son who ran with my granddaughter, too." While Amy's mother didn't run last year
---
because it was too hot, “I got up this morning and I said I
think it’s okay.”

26 year-old Amy Wallace, who graduated from Wake Forest on
a track and cross-country scholarship in 1999, has run this race
once before. “I ran faster last time and came in second. This
time I ran slower and came in first.” Wallace, who lives in
Allston, presently works in a pediatrician’s office in Boston
while she takes classes at Northeastern.

As far as Wallace’s training goes, “I’m dedicated, I ran all
through the winter time when it was negative 10 degrees. Six
o’clock in the morning, every morning, and then go to the gym
after work. All you need to be a runner is tremendous self-
discipline.”

As for the race itself, “I was running with a few guys for
awhile in a little group. Then for the last half-mile I was on
my own.” Did Wallace ever peek over her shoulder to size up the
competition? “Never look behind you!” However, describing
herself more as a distance runner, Amy is looking forward to her
next race, “I’m definitely running Beach to Beacon up in Maine,
a 10K.”

With 238 runners competing in this year’s race the most
ever, Marianne Wronka, a Lynnfield resident who has worked 10 or
more races as a volunteer, was all smiles,

“Last year at this time [because it was so hot] we were
hosing people off [before the race].” The beauty of this race is
that you don’t need to cross the finish line to be a winner.
---
"The goal of this," Wronka says, "is that the money that we raise goes to the Lynnfield Couples Club Scholarship Fund."
The three graduating seniors receiving scholarships, all from Lynnfield High School, are Caila Nickerson, Sarah Gerbick and Richard Palermo Jr. Nickerson, whose mother is a teacher at LHS, is heading to Syracuse. Gerbick, a National Honor Society Member and psychology major, will attend UMass Amherst. You'll get to see Richard Palermo Jr., a business major, jogging with Peter and Steve at UNH.
School Superintendent Richard Palermo achieved the fastest time among male Couple Club members at 20:56 and Susan Beaulieu led the women at 27:01. Richard's wife, Jeannette Palermo, a key organizer of the event, was also all smiles, "I think the race went really well, since it was cooler than last year I think that helped us achieve our biggest turnout to date and we're certainly looking forward to next year's race."
Peter Mallett's advice to anyone looking to take away his title next year: "Run a lot. Run everyday. And you better have trained harder than I did." Or at least as hard as Steve Meinett did?

File name - MH210

Curious about what happens because of the Y2K bug? For a glimpse of the future stop by the computer lab in Meier Hall Room 210.

As you walk in, you briefly survey the scene. There are nine or ten students typing away on their keyboards - typing up reports and E-mailing their friends. The wonderful staff in charge of the lab is busy as well. As well as figuring out why your computer won't print or why you can't log into BobDylan.com they are also using their creativity. I believe that the staff of this computer lab makes better signs than anyone I've ever met, and a lot of them too. A pretty red one reads "out of order". Over in the corner is a computer with two nicely crafted works of art "Not working, Sorry" and "Need new power supply". This is just the beginning, I mentioned the staff's creativity but I neglected to mention their resourcefulness. Immediately on your right as you walk in you see two computers set aside for the physically challenged (yes, another computer made sign complete with color). If you look closely you'll see that on one of them the monitor is being held up with two academic computing books. The last time I checked books were for reading and maybe for holding up the leg of your old broken sofa, not for holding up monitors where someone in a wheelchair might have a hard time getting out of the way if it were to fall. I do admit that it is a resourceful idea, though.

I come into this lab several times a week and don't get me wrong, the staff here does a wonderful job at working with what they have (which at the moment isn't much). If you have a problem, and the odds are you will, they always do the best they can. Six out of the twenty-three computers available to the students aren't functioning correctly. I did the math quickly and it's a little over one/fourth. Considering this is the most highly used lab on campus I expect a little more than that and I think you do too. One thing that I do like is that they have one clock on each side of the room, that way if I forget which side it's on and look hastily I'm bound to see one of them. They also have three fans located strategically around the room. It
---
seems to this untrained eye that a pattern is developing here – what we don't need, they have many of, and what we do need they have few of.

The last couple of weeks they cut their weekly hours from 8:00AM – 11:00PM to 9:00AM – 9:00PM because of a budget cut. I think once word got around that I was doing a story they changed the hours back. That's what I tell people anyway.

Back to the problem; from what I see there are several issues that add to the demise of MH210. First of all, these are the oldest computers at Salem State, so of course, they're bound to have the most problems. Jared Sheffield, Rick Taylor and Jimmy Bartes have the job of fixing all the lab computers on campus. They definitely have their hands full. For example, while writing this article here at MH210, I've had a few "problems". Where do I begin? Well, for the last hour and ten minutes I've had to switch computers four (yes four) times because Microsoft Word would not work properly. But fortunately for me, there were two consecutive the comfy chairs in front of the broken computers and took a nap. It got so bad that Jamie Cowan, a contagiously effervescent computer support specialist, ended up typing my paper over to save me time. I still use the hunt and peck method so sometimes it takes me awhile (and that's aside from the hour and ten minutes wasted because of faulty equipment). Jimmy spent about half an hour searching to find the problem but by the time it was retrieved it resembled hieroglyphics more than an article. This is just a sample of the problems that the staff has to handle everyday. Keep in mind this is just one students troubles during a three hour period.

What is being done about the problem? In an interview with Jared Sheffield I have heard some encouraging news. There is hope for the students and the staff here in Meier Hall 210. There is a plan in the works to fix what problems have within the next couple of weeks. Better still, hopefully all the computers will be replaced by the fall. There was
---
a plan to get the computers from Harrington Building room 100, seeing that there are four labs
there, but things don’t always go as planned. Mr. Sheffield has been on the job since
December and has already fixed many problems, however he is but one man. He maybe good
but it’s hard to move ahead when there’s always a problem of greater importance. “Sometimes
I have to put out fires and when that happens there’s less progress than anticipated,” says
Sheffield. He also stated that he’d rather be challenged than bored, I don’t think he has much
to worry about.
Rick Taylor, the lab supervisor, spends forty hours a week here and estimates that
about thirty of those hours are used troubleshooting the problem(s) of the day. Rick explains
that, “The problem also lies with the students. About 20-30 of them are dangerous and they
mess things up for and the other students.” There have been stories about certain students
sabotaging a computer so that when they come in there is a sign that says broken. They come
right in, sit down and type in the missing command and therefore it’s always available to them.
There have been many students that have been complaining about signing in. Justin
Pagano, E-mail coordinator, expresses the students thoughts quite eloquently “A pound of
flesh, a pint of blood, your first born son and three forms of I.D.” What must be remembered is
that the lab attendants, like Justin, do not make the rules they only enforce them. The reason
for the inconvenience is that this is used as a safeguard against those who do not conform to
the rules. If something goes wrong then the attendants are held responsible. It seems that they
are always held responsible. Jamie Cowan sees this problem quite frequently, “Recently we
have been getting a lot of angry people, particularly night students, who come into the lab and
take their frustrations out on the attendants. We simply refuse to let a student use the
computers until he/she can show us adequate proof. When they come in with an attitude,
swearing at us and kicking doors, we call campus police and ban them from the lab for the rest
of the semester.”
---
The attendants also want to remind you to always bring a disk and save your work every so often. If you're unsure of something try looking around the room at the numerous signs because not only are they pretty but they also serve a purpose. There is hope, but if the lab stays this way for too long contact Salem State's president Nancy Harrington and voice your opinion.

Tom Jensen

WORDS:
WELLNESS by Tom Jensen

What is wellness? That is certainly a good question to start with when one is trying to decide how well one's well is. I would consider wellness the successful achievement of one limiting one's negative characteristics and traits. By limiting the negative in one's collective body and soul the effect, therefore, is accenting the positive. Addition by subtraction if you will. So, since coming to the very real acceptance of who I am and what I do I am able to make a judgment over how well is my wellness. What flaws have been noticed, studied, and fixed? What traits have I stepped back from my eyes and observed from another frame of reference? How have I felt about my relationships with friends and family? What have I yet to achieve on the Totem Pole of life, how far have I climbed? All things of this nature make for interesting talk and type but the main element one has to remember is that all of these subjects are subjective to the observer. Anyone may relate oneself to others in an attempt to compare actions and sometimes even justify an unjust act. One's immediate circle acts as the shell in which the egg is kept. On one hand, the shell can protect the egg from predators, harm and frying pans but the shell also succeeds in limiting how far the egg can expand and thereby cut off the egg from the far away chicken of happiness. I am the egg man, sorry Mr. Lennon.

But, as the more I learn the more I see how correct my poetry can be. It seems society has reached the point where it can no longer envision evil and therefore attempt to prevent evil from happening in the first place. It is only after the original act has been done that the necessary corrections are deemed worthy.

Cannot fix the flaw - only patch the hole
The potential of diamonds results in coal
Abie to race the race though blind to the goal
Only glimpses and pieces never the whole

I am living the paradox which is the same as society. I am able to see the goal ahead of me. I am well aware of my major flaws and I certainly do hold the potential for greatness and diamonds. That is the good part. The problem lies in the fact that I am aware of the flaw but I choose to only patch the hole. Never giant changes, only small subtleties which meagerly reshape my path towards
---
the future. The dark side of the diamond shows his grim face. In life, knowledge is the ultimate power but how should one feel if he is the knower yet not the doer? So many ignorant fools would die to think just one great thought. Why take it for granted when one has so much to share in so little time? This is the dilemma of the people caught in the trap.

My wellness is as it finds me, finds me as I have been, in the same structure, same form. Faces change just as does the weather. My feet are always moving but it’s not always up. A life which was created and I now call my own. A time when the only time one can truly take the time to gather one’s inner thoughts is a time when is only an afterthought. A busy productive day only ends in an even busier unproductive night. Voices have warmed me and wisdom has guided these voices. The face has a name and the deed is a game. Just as the earth spins so does a day as patterns emerge and it takes more to wash away a sand castle than just a single wave. Or so the saying goes...

ODE TO COREY (A FALLEN HERO)

This is a story about a boy who's dog ran away
Who, during a snow storm, went out to play
Corey set out to find a loved one - no matter what the cost
But as the dog came home the little boy became lost
When you're a fourth grader finding a dog is no easy task
Should you risk your life for a pet? It depends on who you ask
The fact that Corey said yes should come as no surprise
He loved that dog to pieces you could see it in his eyes
Little Corey was a hero so he set out through the snow
It saddens my heart deeply to tell his tale of woe
What a brave little soul, right up until the end
What a brave little soul to go search for his friend
A little bit of inspiration is what he left behind
He listened to his heart, paid no attention to his mind
And right before he left our world with the situation oh so grim
The last thought that filled his head - his dog would do the same for him
The saddest of it all and the reason why we cried
If not for the heart of an angel he never would have died
When you think of him in memory try to wipe away your tears
And remember him for what he was which is wise beyond his years

Tom Jensen January 27, 1999 Creative Writing A Hard Rain's Gonna Fall

The smoke from a half lit cigarette waves aimlessly through the air. A light brown guitar sits in the corner awaiting the delicate touch of its master. Three empty notebooks sit atop the table curiously wondering what will fill their blank pages. Will there be small sketches of beautiful young women or perhaps some silly verses about how everybody must get stoned? An old weathered, green chair, still feeling the pain of a dropped cigarette, reminisces about the time it's owner, the master, once sat for what seemed like an eternity trying to capture the soul of a man named Hollis Brown. An old, rusty razor lays, forgotten, in a corner clutching on to one piece of cocaine. A broken guitar string sits beneath a pile of trash still humming the melody of what it prays comes true in "Forever Young", and in the state of mind that it will never be thrown away.

A familiar face appears from behind a closed door. All of the objects in the room experience a buzz of excitement. Perhaps one of them will receive their master's attention, if even only for an instant. The master sits upon the green chair and sighs. "Must be another sad love song", the chair thinks to itself. The razor, on the other hand says, "I think he's angry at the world, I hope he's not as angry as that 'Masters of war' song...You know, the one that goes:

And I hope that you die

And you're death'll come soon

I will follow your casket

In the pale afternoon

And I'll watch while you're lowered

Down to your deathbed

And I'll stand o'er your grave '

Til I'm sure that you're dead

The master grabs the yellow notebook and begins jotting down a few lines. The guitar waits patiently, for it knows that the master always uses him and the notebook together. As plain as bread and butter and as sweet as peanut butter and jelly. After a little while, just like clockwork, the notebook is set aside and the inevitable happens. A quick tuning and he's off. "What'd he write, can you see?" asks the guitar, even though he'll be one of the first ones to hear. To which the notebook responds, "It's kinda hard to see considering everything's upside down but it looks like it says..." At that very instance the master begins strumming along and starts singing softly:

"Boy, were we off!" shouts the guitar, over the loud playing. "Sounds like a happy song."

After a quick cigarette and a half of joint the master begins to think to himself. He wonders to himself if all the pain and sacrifice of all his endless nights of writing and playing are worth it. He wonders what will fill the next blank page. He remembers the night he turned heads as his audience watched (some in anger that he "sold out" and others in enjoyment) as he magically blended folk and rock into one. He remembers the boos, the cheers, and all the fans over the years. A smile is brought to his face as he thinks of going from playing in corner coffee shops in New York all the way to the big time.

He thinks of the night in the Chelsea Hotel writing "Sad-eyed Lady of the lowlands" for his wife Sarah The master sits back in his chair, puts his feet on the table and stares at his pen as stares deliberately at his pen as if looking for inspiration. The pens screams out inaudibly, "I love you, man!" But alas. The master cannot hear these words of love, though, he just continues staring at the pen.

The master then begins thinking about his almost fateful motorcycle crash and begins humming something about "knocking on heaven's door". The old, rusty razor yells with pride, "He used me that night, my God! I didn't sleep for a week!" The notebook, always of good humor, responds, "HELL, you could have killed him right there!" The master is always the center of attention in this room, as you might expect. Of course, being the greatest of all time can have that effect on people, er... things.

As the master sits about to take a little rest he began to pick up a magazine in which he has been quoted. He ponders the ups and downs of being famous and all of the expectations that come with it. He reads his dialogue from an article about him, "You can't try to come up with songs that people will think is all hip and cool, you have to write for yourself. There are too many phonies out there and all the one hit wonders. They come up with a gimmick catch phrase, write some mumbo jumbo and the people love it. Six months later they've blown all their dough and the fans never even knew who they were."

As he gazes out the window at the pouring rain out side the master wonders again who exactly he is writing for,
---
who are the ones who really enjoy his work. He doesn't realize that his biggest fan is sitting right here in this room, it is 
actually his guitar. The two make a marvelous pair, not unlike the guitar and the notebook. Sometimes in this world in 
which we live in things are not always what they seem. This is the reason that the master continues with his work-to 
explain the unseen, to show what is right, what is pure and true and consequentially, what is wrong and needs to be 
changed. So with his aging face, fading voice and wearing guitar he carries on with no direction home, like a rolling stone. 
He knows how it feels to have to seek shelter from the storm. He is aware that the times they are a'changing and he's 
spreading the word to the uninformed. With that thought he begins to sing a few verses from one of his songs:

Stake my future on a hell of a past

Looks like tomorrow is coming on fast

Ain't complainin' 'bout what I got

Seen better times but who has not....

The guitar understands the master's thoughts as they have been partners for many years. If not for anyone else, he has 
been touched by their many nights together. The guitar has experienced what life outside the room is like through the 
master's music and is happy inside the dry, warm room. For the master has predicted that a hard rain's gonna fall and 
when you're made of wood you can't really hold an umbrella can you?

As the master is getting ready to lay down for a night's rest he happens to realize that he was sitting on one of his 
albums: SELF PORTRAIT by Bob Dylan. And on that note he falls asleep contently remembering what someone 
once said to him, "Don't think twice, it's alright."

Here is the premise of my argument against the retiring of Tony
Conigliaro's number: The Red Sox have only retired five numbers in their ninety-
plus year history and the numbers that Tony C. put up while he was healthy are
not as good as comparable Red Sox Hall of Fame and number retiree hopefuls
Jim Rice and Dwight Evans. In a nutshell, Tony C. was a baseball player with an
incredibly high ceiling who was tragically beaned in the prime of his career,
resulting in his career being shortened and ultimately finished. Cincinnati Reds
first baseman Tony Perez has been inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame and
had his jersey retired by the Reds. Take a look at the statistics and pretend
you're the general manager of a team looking to make a big trade. If you could
trade for just one of these four players which one would you want? What if you
could retire just one of their numbers, who deserves it the most?
Jim Rice played in Boston for 16 years and Dwight Evans for 18. Tony C.
was here for just over six seasons. Will I be angered if the Red Sox retire Tony's

Lynn, Dwight Evans, Duffy Lewis, Waite Hoyt, Johnny Pesky, Luis Aparicio, Tom

Jefferson’s vision of America and the America he ended his presidency
with were far from the same. The financial America was far to complex and
interdependent to ever concede to the agrarian society Jefferson dreamed of.
The Louisiana Purchase gave Americans increasing opportunity to venture West
in search of their own dreams and escape. Jefferson did significantly reduce the
powers of the central government and heighten state government but he could
never limit Americans to a self-dependent farming nature as a boom in
technology and a boom in population would not allow for the change. The
Jeffersonian deficit was cut by one third and he reduced the government’s
money by a significant portion.
---
Jefferson's legacy will be forever view as a dual complexity. The man who drafted the Declaration of Independence came from a family of Southern slave owners. Jefferson weakened the Federal government yet many times had to use strong national authority. In some cases, his administration used even more power than the Federalists before him did. Jefferson's Republics realized that America was changing fast and that the idea of being an isolated nation was only an idea.
